broadcast.title: 2. Broadcasting: Combining Arrays of Different Shapes
broadcast.intro: Broadcasting lets NumPy compute A + B even when the shapes differ, without copying any data. Choose two shapes, walk through the rule one axis at a time, and see which value each result cell uses.

story.outer: A column (3,1) meets a row (1,4): each side stretches along its length-1 axis and they fill a 3×4 grid.
story.row: Subtract one value per column from every row. This is how X − X.mean(axis=0) centers each feature.
story.scalar: A scalar has shape (), so it broadcasts to any shape: every element is multiplied by the same number.
story.mismatch: Trailing axes 4 and 3 differ and neither is 1, so NumPy raises an error. See the suggested fix below.
story.silent: Looks like adding two 3-element vectors, but (3,) acts as a row and (3,1) as a column, so the result is 3×3. No error is raised.
story.cube: B (3,1) is stretched along the last axis and repeated for both blocks of A.

broadcast.rule_title: Step 1 · Check the shapes axis by axis (right to left)

narr.align: Write {{a}} and {{b}} right-aligned. If one shape has fewer axes, pad it with 1s on the left (marked 1⁺). Then compare one column at a time, starting from the last axis.
narr.equal: Axis {{axis}}: both lengths are {{a}}. They are equal, so the result also has length {{out}} here.
narr.stretchA: Axis {{axis}}: A has length 1, B has {{b}}. A's single value is reused {{out}} times along this axis.
narr.stretchB: Axis {{axis}}: B has length 1, A has {{a}}. B's single value is reused {{out}} times along this axis.
narr.mismatch: Axis {{axis}}: {{a}} vs {{b}}. They differ and neither is 1, so broadcasting fails here.
narr.done_ok: Every axis is compatible, so the result shape is {{shape}}.
narr.done_fail: Incompatible at axis {{axis}}: NumPy raises a ValueError.

broadcast.memory_desc: A stride of 0 means moving along that axis re-reads the same element, so the stretched operands are free. Only {{a}} + {{b}} values are stored; NumPy allocates memory just for the {{out}}-element result.
broadcast.error_title: operands could not be broadcast together
broadcast.fix: Fix: add a length-1 axis, turning {{from}} into {{to}}:

cards.rule_1: Line the shapes up on the right.
cards.rule_2: Compare each axis: the lengths must be equal, or one of them must be 1.
cards.rule_3: A missing axis counts as 1. The result takes the larger length on each axis.
cards.mem: A length-1 axis is stretched by giving it stride 0, which re-reads the same value instead of copying it. Code like X - mu is therefore both shorter and faster than a Python loop.

cards.pit: A 1-D array of shape (3,) behaves like a row. Combining it with a (3,1) column gives a 3×3 matrix instead of 3 values, and NumPy raises no error. Check .shape, and write a[:, None] or a.reshape(-1, 1) when you mean a column.

broadcast.advice: Broadcasting doesn't actually copy data in memory, but virtually maps addresses during iteration. Core rule: Compare from the last dimension forward, they must either be equal or one of them is <1>1</1>.

pairwise.title: 3. Pairwise Distance in One NumPy Line (Exam Video)
pairwise.intro: A short animated video on a question that keeps coming back in COMP2211 papers: compute every test-to-train distance with no loops. It uses the exact data from the 2022 Spring midterm Q2(c) and follows the official marking scheme, tracking the shape at every step.

pairwise.keys: Click the video to play or pause. Keyboard: Space plays or pauses, ← / → move between scenes. Click a chapter to jump to it.

pairwise.advice: Every year this shows up as KNN or K-Means "without loops": 2022S Q2(c) for Euclidean distance, 2023F for Minkowski + np.argsort(…, axis=1)[:, :k], 2023S for a Poincaré distance with np.expand_dims. Marks go to the shape change, the right axis in sum / argsort, and the (num_test, num_train) order. Write the shape as a comment after every step; that alone catches most mistakes.

question.title: The exam question
question.c1: This exact task was in the COMP2211 2022 Spring midterm (Q2c, 9 points): rewrite a nested-loop distance function with no explicit loops.
question.c2: The marking scheme is blunt: any for loop or list comprehension scores 0. You need the one-line broadcasting trick.
question.c3: Here is the answer we are going to build. Let's take it apart and track the shape at every step.

data.title: What we want
data.c1: X_test holds 2 points and X_train holds 4, each with 2 coordinates: shapes (2, 2) and (4, 2).
data.c2: We need the distance between every test point and every train point: 2 × 4 = 8 numbers.
data.c3: Row i is test point i and column j is train point j, so the answer has shape (num_test, num_train) = (2, 4). Getting it the wrong way round costs a mark.

line.title: The one line
line.c1: Read it from the inside out: five operations, and only the first one is tricky.
line.c2: The shape goes (2, 2) & (4, 2) → (2, 4, 2) → (2, 4). The 3-D middle step holds all 8 pairs at once.

fail.title: Why X_test − X_train fails
fail.c1: First instinct: just subtract. NumPy compares shapes from the right, and the last axis is fine: 2 vs 2.
fail.c2: But then 2 test rows meet 4 train rows. They differ and neither is 1, so NumPy raises a ValueError.
fail.c3: If the counts happened to match, it would be worse: no error, just the wrong pairs. Under the marking scheme, no shape change scores 0 of the 4 subtraction points.

axes.title: Insert a new axis
axes.c1: The fix is to give each array its own axis. None (= np.newaxis) inserts an axis of length 1 where you write it.
axes.c2: X_test[:, None, :] is (2, 1, 2), with test points down axis 0. X_train[None, :, :] is (1, 4, 2), with train points along axis 1.
axes.c3: Broadcasting will stretch the 1s. np.expand_dims(X_test, 1) does the same thing, and X_train[None] is optional because NumPy pads missing axes on the left.

broadcast.title: Broadcast: (2, 4, 2)
broadcast.c1: Compare (2, 1, 2) with (1, 4, 2): the last axes match, and in each of the other two one side is 1. Both arrays can stretch.
broadcast.c2: Test points are reused across the 4 columns and train points down the 2 rows. Nothing is copied in memory: the stretched axis has stride 0.
broadcast.c3: Cell [i, j] now holds X_test[i] − X_train[j]. That is all 8 difference vectors at once, shape (2, 4, 2).

reduce.title: Square, then sum axis = −1
reduce.c1: Square every coordinate difference: (5, 5) becomes (25, 25). The shape stays (2, 4, 2).
reduce.c2: Sum along the last axis, the coordinate axis, so each cell collapses to one number: (2, 4, 2) → (2, 4).
reduce.c3: axis=2 and axis=-1 are both right. axis=1 adds up different train points and gives (2, 2): it runs, but the result means nothing. The scheme deducts a point for a missing or wrong axis.

result.title: sqrt → the distance matrix
result.c1: Apply np.sqrt element by element. The shape stays (2, 4), and these are exactly the numbers printed in the exam paper.
result.c2: Row i lists test point i's distance to every train point, so KNN takes np.argsort(D, axis=1)[:, :k]. The 2023 Fall midterm asked exactly this, with Minkowski distance.
result.c3: Here train point r3 at (3, 4) is the nearest neighbour of both test points.

recap.title: Exam checklist
recap.c1: This is the shape trail. In the exam, write it as comments next to your code.
recap.c2: Check each item before you hand in. Most lost marks come from a missing axis or the wrong axis.
recap.c3: The (n, m, d) middle array is the price of the one-liner. Now run the code yourself below.

data.cell: D[i, j] = distance(test i, train j)

fail.silent: Silent trap: with 4 test and 4 train points, X_test − X_train runs without error but only pairs row i with row i, giving 4 differences instead of 16.

axes.pad: missing axes are padded on the left

broadcast.ghost: Dashed = virtual copies made by broadcasting (stride 0)

result.match: matches the output printed in the exam paper

recap.no_loop: No for loop and no list comprehension, or the answer scores 0
recap.axis: Insert the axis: X_test[:, None] or np.expand_dims(X_test, 1)
recap.square: Square the difference (a − b)², not a² − b²
recap.sum: Sum over the last axis: axis=-1 (or 2)
recap.memory: Memory: the (n, m, d) intermediate costs n·m·d numbers. For large data, the official solution expands ‖x − y‖² = ‖x‖² + ‖y‖² − 2x·y and uses one matrix product, X_test @ X_train.T, so no 3-D array is ever built.

fire_case.title: 2. Practice: Smoke & Fire Case (Notes P.15)
fire_case.advice: Classic case from notes: Fire is rare (Prior=1%), but smoke is common (Marginal=10%, maybe BBQ). Bayes tells us probability of fire given smoke is only <1>9\%</1>. <3>Evidence ≠ Conclusion, Prior matters!</3>
fire_case.evidence_bound: By total probability <1></1>, so P(Smoke) cannot go below P(Smoke|Fire)·P(Fire) = {{v}}% — otherwise the posterior would exceed 100%.

naive.advice: Key point from Notes P.23: Bayes is 'Naive' because it assumes features are <1>conditionally independent</1>. Efficient for spam filtering. Watch out for <3>Zero Frequency Problem</3>, increase <5>\alpha</5> to see changes!
naive.zero_warning: A zero count makes the whole product 0 (log 0 = −∞), so that class can never win whatever the other features say. Increase <1></1> to smooth it away.

exam_tip.title: Exam Tip
exam_tip.content_numpy: Exam Note: <1>Broadcasting</1> can only extend dimensions of Size 1. <3>A \cdot B</3> (np.dot) and <5>A \odot B</5> (Element-wise) have completely different physical meanings!
exam_tip.content_backprop: Exam Note: error flows backward — compute <1>\delta_k</1> at the output layer first. Memorize <3>\Delta w = \eta \delta O</3> and mind the sign of (T - O)!
exam_tip.content_kernel: Exam Note: with no padding and stride 1, output size is <1>N - K + 1</1>. Sobel-X responds to vertical edges — don't mix up the direction!
exam_tip.content_bayesBasics: Exam Note: <1>P(B|E) \propto P(B) \cdot P(E|B)</1>. The denominator P(E) only normalizes — compare hypotheses by the numerator!
exam_tip.content_naiveBayes: Exam Note: one zero frequency kills the whole product — apply <1>\alpha</1> smoothing. With many features, switch to <3>\log</3> sums to avoid underflow!
exam_tip.content_knn: Exam Note: choose an odd <1>K</1> to avoid tie votes, and always standardize features — otherwise large-range features dominate the distance!
exam_tip.content_alphabeta: Exam Note: pruning fires when <1>\beta \le \alpha</1>. Node visiting order matters — <3>a good move ordering prunes far more branches</3>!
exam_tip.content_kmeans: Exam Note: every iteration keeps <1>WCSS</1> non-increasing, so K-Means always converges — but only to a local optimum (initialization matters). Pick <3>K</3> at the elbow point!
exam_tip.content_perceptron: Exam Note: the update <1>w \leftarrow w + \eta\, y\, x</1> fires only on misclassified points — and converges only if the data is linearly separable!
exam_tip.content_pytorch: Exam Note: the training trio order matters — <1>\text{zero\_grad} \to \text{backward} \to \text{step}</1>. Forget zero_grad and gradients accumulate!

rule.create: Builds a new array from scratch — there is no input array to trace.

rule.move: Nothing is computed: every result cell is a copy of exactly one input cell. Hover to see which one.
rule.move_many: Nothing is computed: each result cell is copied from one of the {{n}} input arrays (tinted by origin).
rule.elementwise: Each result cell uses only the matching cell of each input. Shapes {{shapes}} are broadcast to {{out}} first.
rule.reduce_all: All {{n}} values collapse into a single number ({{op}}).
rule.reduce_axis: axis={{axis}}: the {{len}} values along axis {{axis}} collapse into one ({{op}}), so {{from}} becomes {{to}}.
rule.scan_flat: Running total over the flattened array: each cell is the sum of itself and everything before it.
rule.scan_axis: Running total along axis {{axis}}: each cell adds up everything before it in its lane.
rule.matmul: result[i, j] = row i of the left × column j of the right, multiplied pairwise and summed ({{k}} products).
rule.outer: result[i, j] = a[i] × b[j] — every pair, no summing.
rule.sort: Values are rearranged along axis {{axis}}; hover a cell to see where it came from.
rule.sort_flat: The whole array is flattened and sorted; hover a cell to see where it came from.
rule.argsort: argsort returns positions, not values: each number says where the k-th smallest value sits in the input.
rule.unique: Each distinct value once, sorted. Hover one to see every place it occurs.
rule.linalg: Every result cell depends on the whole matrix — there is no cell-by-cell shortcut.
rule.poly_create: A polynomial is just its coefficients, lowest degree first: [1, 2, 3] means 1 + 2x + 3x².
rule.poly_eval: Calling p(x) plugs x into the polynomial; the red dots are the values it returned.
rule.poly_deriv: The derivative (solid) is zero exactly where the original curve (dashed) turns around.
rule.poly_integ: The integral (solid) grows where the original (dashed) is positive and shrinks where it is negative.
rule.poly_roots: Roots are where the curve crosses zero. If it never crosses, the roots are complex and nothing can be marked.
rule.poly_convert: Fitted polynomials live on a shifted, scaled x; convert() rewrites them with ordinary x coefficients.
rule.poly_fit: Least squares: the curve that makes the total squared vertical gap to the points as small as possible.
rule.poly_arith: Polynomials combine with + − * ** like numbers; the solid curve is the result.
rule.polyfit: Legacy API: same least-squares fit, but the coefficients come back highest degree first.
rule.polyval: Legacy API: evaluates coefficients given highest degree first.

api.array: Turns a (nested) Python list into an array; the nesting depth becomes the number of axes.
api.arange: Evenly spaced integers like range(): the stop value is excluded.
api.linspace: A fixed number of evenly spaced points; both ends are included.
api.zeros: An array of a given shape filled with 0 (or 1 with np.ones); float unless you pass dtype.
api.full: An array of a given shape filled with one value.
api.eye: The identity matrix: 1 on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere.
api.zeros_like: Same shape and dtype as an existing array, but filled with 0.
api.reshape: Same values in the same order, new shape. Values are read row by row (C order).
api.reshape_neg: Put -1 for one axis and NumPy works out its length from the total size.
api.ravel: Flattens to 1-D in row order. ravel returns a view when it can; flatten always copies.
api.transpose: Swaps rows and columns: result[i, j] = a[j, i]. No data is copied.
api.swapaxes: Swaps two chosen axes of an N-D array.
api.expand_dims: Inserts a new axis of length 1 — the trick behind broadcasting a vector against every row.
api.concatenate: Joins arrays end to end along an existing axis; the other axes must match.
api.stack: Joins equal-shape arrays along a NEW axis, so the result has one more dimension.
api.vstack: vstack stacks rows on top of each other; hstack puts them side by side.
api.tile: Repeats the whole array like floor tiles.
api.repeat: Repeats each element (or row/column) in place.
api.flip: Reverses the order along an axis (all axes if none given). Returns a view.
api.slice: Basic slicing start:stop:step on each axis returns a view of the original.
api.fancy: Integer arrays pick arbitrary cells; paired lists give (row, col) points. Always a copy.
api.mask: A boolean array keeps the cells where it is True, flattened in row order.
api.where: np.where(cond, x, y) takes x where cond is True and y elsewhere, cell by cell.
api.broadcast: Arrays of different shapes combine after stretching length-1 axes — no copies are made.
api.scalar_op: Arithmetic with a scalar applies to every element.
api.compare: Comparisons give a boolean array, ready to use as a mask.
api.sqrt: Universal functions (ufuncs) apply to every element independently.
api.maximum: Element-wise larger of two arrays (or array and scalar) — np.maximum(z, 0) is ReLU.
api.clip: Limits every value to the range [low, high].
api.round: Rounds to the nearest value; exact halves go to the even neighbour (0.5 → 0, 1.5 → 2).
api.abs: Element-wise absolute value; np.square squares every element.
api.sum: Sums along one axis. axis=0 collapses rows (one result per column), axis=1 collapses columns.
api.sum_all: With no axis, every element is added into one number.
api.mean: Average along an axis — here one mean per row.
api.max: Largest value along an axis; np.min gives the smallest.
api.argmax: Position of the largest value along an axis — the predicted class for each row of probabilities.
api.std: Standard deviation along an axis. NumPy divides by n (ddof=0) unless you ask otherwise.
api.prod: Multiplies the values along an axis.
api.cumsum: Running total: each cell is the sum of everything up to it.
api.any: any: is at least one value True? all: are they all True? — along an axis.
api.count_nonzero: Counts the non-zero (True) cells — handy for counting correct predictions.
api.sort: Returns a sorted copy along an axis (the last axis by default).
api.argsort: Returns the indices that would sort the array — the core of KNN's nearest neighbours.
api.matmul: Matrix product: rows of the left times columns of the right. The inner lengths must match.
api.matvec: Matrix times vector: one dot product per row, e.g. a linear model's predictions.
api.outer: Every element of a times every element of b.
api.norm: Euclidean length: square, sum, square root — along an axis or over everything.
api.inv: Matrix inverse: A @ inv(A) gives the identity (up to rounding).
api.det: Determinant of a square matrix; 0 means it has no inverse.
api.rand: Uniform random numbers in [0, 1) with the given shape.
api.randint: Random integers from low (included) to high (excluded).
api.randn: Samples from the standard normal distribution (mean 0, std 1).
api.poly_note: The code block from this note, made runnable (q is defined here). Step through the calls to see each result.
api.poly_eval: Evaluate a polynomial at one value or a whole array at once.
api.poly_deriv: Differentiate (deriv) or integrate (integ) and get a new Polynomial back.
api.poly_roots: All roots of the polynomial, sorted; complex ones are returned as complex numbers.
api.poly_fit: Fit a polynomial of a chosen degree to noisy data, then convert() to read the coefficients.
api.polyfit: The old np.polyfit: coefficients highest degree first — for degree 1 that is [slope, intercept].

perc.lead: Feed one row at a time: compute O, and only if it is wrong move w and θ by η(T − O)x. Watch the decision line jump until every point is on its side — or never, if no straight line exists.

course.title: Exam-style: course ratings
course.note: Pattern of 2022 Fall Q6 — f = 1 only if z > 0

pm.title: Exam-style: ±1 outputs
pm.note: Pattern of 2022 Spring Q6 — f = 1 if z ≥ 0 else −1

perc.plot_aria: Training points and the current decision line
perc.line_sub: blue side → output high · dashed = before this row
perc.start_text: Start: w = {{w}}, θ = {{theta}}, η = {{eta}}. Press <1>Next row</1>.
perc.converged: Epoch {{n}} made no changes, so every row is classified correctly. The data is linearly separable.
perc.no_conv: The weights keep changing. If no straight line can separate the classes (XOR), the perceptron rule never stops.
perc.epoch_note: An epoch has converged only when a <1>whole pass</1> makes no update — an exam answer of “not converged in 1 epoch” needs exactly that reason.
perc.activation: Papers disagree: lecture 5 and 2022 Spring output high when z ≥ 0, 2022 Fall only when z > 0, and outputs may be 0/1 or −1/+1. With −1/+1 outputs a mistake gives T − O = ±2, so the step doubles. Rows that land exactly on z = 0 are where students lose marks.
perc.separable: The perceptron convergence theorem: if a separating line exists, this rule finds one in finitely many updates. If none exists (XOR, or “success iff both ratings are 2 or 3” in 2022 Fall), you need a hidden layer — see the next page.

xor.lead: A single neuron draws one straight line, and XOR needs two. A hidden layer draws two lines, squashes the plane, and in the new (h₁, h₂) space one line is enough. Backpropagation finds those weights δ by δ.

hand.title: Hand-picked weights (step)
hand.note: Pattern of 2023 Spring Q7(c) / 2025 Spring Q7 — OR & NAND → AND

zeros.title: All weights zero
zeros.note: Final 2022 Q3(d): why zero init fails

xor.input_aria: Network output over the input plane
xor.step_title: No training with a step function.
xor.step_note: Its gradient is 0 almost everywhere, so backprop has nothing to follow (Final 2024 Q4c). The fix: a steep sigmoid σ(cx) approximates the step and still has a gradient.
xor.solved: All four points fall on the right side. Look at the hidden-space plot: the hidden layer moved (0,1) and (1,0) to one side of a single straight line — that is exactly what the 2023 Spring hint (“make the points linearly separable after the first layer”) asks you to construct.
xor.unsolved: Some points are still misclassified. Train more, or adjust weights by hand until the hidden-space plot becomes separable by one line.
xor.symmetric: Both hidden units have identical weights, so they always compute the same value and receive the same δ — they can never become different. This is why all-zero initialisation fails.
xor.hidden_delta_note: Hidden δ uses w5 and w6 <1>before</1> this step’s update, as on the lecture slides. With the lecture start, round 1 gives δk = 0.107022 and new w5 = 0.833245.
xor.loss_sub: ½(T − O)² averaged over the 4 samples
xor.overshoot: A very large η can overshoot and oscillate instead of settling.
xor.wb_note: every non-input neuron has one weight per input plus one bias
xor.traps: The course writes δk = (O − T)·O(1 − O) and <1>subtracts</1>: w ← w − ηδO. Some books write (T − O) and add — same result, but use the paper’s convention. With a <2>linear</2> activation, stacking layers adds nothing: the whole network collapses to one neuron (2022 Spring Q7b).
xor.output_note: Binary: 1 sigmoid unit. Multi-class: softmax over n units. Multi-label: n sigmoid units (Final 2022). Never ReLU at the output of a classifier: its range is unbounded, so there is no natural cut-off.

flip.why: the value comes from a different position

affine.lead: Every geometric transform in lecture 7 is one 2 × 3 matrix M: [x′, y′] = M · [x, y, 1]. Pick a transform, click any output pixel to see where its value came from, and check which properties survive.

translate.title: Translation
translate.note: x′ = x + tx, y′ = y + ty

rotate.title: Rotation about the centre
rotate.note: about (cols // 2, rows // 2), as in the lecture code

shear.title: Shear
shear.note: x′ = x + k·y: squares become parallelograms

affine.rotate_dir: The y-axis points down, so a positive θ turns the picture counter-clockwise on screen — the same as cv2.getRotationMatrix2D.
affine.dsize: dsize is (cols, rows) — width first — while img.shape is (rows, cols). Swapping them is a classic bug.
affine.pixels_sub: Click a pixel on the right
affine.came_from: Output pixel <1>({{x}}, {{y}})</1> takes its value from input pixel <3>({{sx}}, {{sy}})</3> = {{v}}. warpAffine walks the output and looks each pixel up through M⁻¹; the forward map alongside sends that input pixel to its new place.
affine.outside: Output pixel <1>({{x}}, {{y}})</1> maps back to a point outside the input, so warpAffine fills it with borderValue = 0 (hatched).
affine.legend: x is the column and y is the row, with (0, 0) at the top-left. Hatched cells came from outside the image. The red dot marks the rotation / scaling centre. Non-integer results are rounded to the nearest pixel (cv2.INTER_NEAREST).
affine.corners_note: Plug each corner into x′ = a₀₀x + a₀₁y + b₀₀ and y′ = a₁₀x + a₁₁y + b₁₀. For a reflection, a corner must land on another corner — the − 1 in rows − 1 is what makes that happen.
affine.keeps_note: Every affine map keeps lines straight and parallel and keeps midpoints. Distances and angles are kept only by some of them (translation, rotation, reflection), so “an affine transformation may preserve distances and angles” is TRUE.
affine.lattice_aria: Grid lines and a right triangle before (grey) and after (blue) the linear part of M
affine.by3_yes: Every output pixel copies the same neighbour at most one pixel away, so a 3 × 3 kernel with a single 1 in the right place does it.
affine.by3_no: A 3 × 3 kernel only sees the pixel and its 8 neighbours, the same way everywhere. This transform needs values from far away, or from a different offset at each position — so no kernel can do it. For a 64 × 64 flip the farthest source is 63 pixels away.
affine.not_point: An affine transformation is not a point operation: the output at (x, y) comes from a different position. Final 2022 Q1(f) (“Otsu and affine transformations are point-based”) is FALSE for that reason. A flip does keep the histogram, though, because no value changes.

cnn.strip_title: Where does the output size come from?
cnn.rules: Conv: (k·k·C<1>in</1> + 1) × filters — the depth of the input counts, the image size does not. Pooling, Flatten and Dropout have none. Dense: (inputs + 1) × units. The +1 is the bias; leave it out only if the paper says “no bias”.
cnn.why: One kernel is reused at every position (parameter sharing), and each output only looks at a small window (sparse connections). A dense layer needs a separate weight for every pixel — see the MLP preset. Changing the input size breaks the first dense layer unless a global pooling layer squeezes the map to 1 × 1 first (Final 2023 Q6f).

cnn.keras_note: Keras only knows padding="valid" (no border) or "same"; an explicit border of p pixels needs ZeroPadding2D first. input_shape goes on the first layer only, channels last, without the batch size — summary() shows the batch as None.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Exam after exam asks the same question: why can a single perceptron not learn XOR, and what does a hidden layer change?

points.title: Four points
points.c1: XOR has just four inputs. It outputs 1 when exactly one of x₁, x₂ is 1 — blue — and 0 otherwise — red.
points.c2: Put them on the plane: the blue points sit on one diagonal, the red points on the other.
points.c3: A single neuron computes step(w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b). Its boundary w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = 0 is one straight line.

lines.title: Try every line
lines.c1: So let us try lines. Every position, every angle.
lines.c2: Some get two points right, many get three. Watch the best score.
lines.c3: It never reaches four. Three out of four is the best any straight line can do.
lines.ponder: Before the next chapter: can you prove no line works, using only four inequalities?

proof.title: The four-line proof
proof.c1: Write down what each point demands from w₁, w₂ and b.
proof.c2: (0,0) must give 0, so b ≤ 0. The two blue points need w₁ + b > 0 and w₂ + b > 0.
proof.c3: Add those two: w₁ + w₂ + 2b > 0, so w₁ + w₂ + b > −b, which is at least 0.
proof.c4: But (1,1) must give 0, so w₁ + w₂ + b ≤ 0. Contradiction. This is the full-mark answer to 2025 Spring Q7(c).

idea.title: Change the question
idea.c1: If no line fits the points, change the points. That is exactly what a hidden layer does.
idea.c2: Each hidden neuron computes a new coordinate. The output neuron then draws its line in that new space, not in the original one.

stretch.title: Step 1: a linear map
stretch.c1: First the weights: z = 3(Wx + c). Watch the whole grid move with it.
stretch.c2: A linear map can stretch, shear and shift the plane…
stretch.c3: …but straight lines stay straight and parallel lines stay parallel.
stretch.c4: So the points are still not separable. A linear step alone changes nothing — which is why the activation matters.

squash.title: Step 2: the sigmoid squash
squash.c1: Now the activation. σ squeezes every number into the range 0 to 1.
squash.c2: Applied to both coordinates, it squashes the stretched plane into the unit square. The grid lines bend.
squash.c3: The red point (1,1) is pushed to the top-right corner, (0,0) to the bottom-left edge, and both blue points end up near the bottom right.

separate.title: Step 3: one straight line
separate.c1: Here are the four points in hidden space, with their new coordinates.
separate.c2: The output neuron draws one straight line: y = step(h₁ − h₂ − 0.4).
separate.c3: Both blue points are on one side, both red points on the other. XOR solved.
separate.c4: Look at the corners: h₁ behaves like OR, h₂ like AND, and the output says “OR but not AND” — which is XOR.
separate.ponder: Why does the activation have to be non-linear? What would happen to the bent grid without σ?

pullback.title: Back in the input plane
pullback.c1: Let us carry that straight line back through the network: undo the squash…
pullback.c2: …undo the stretch, and colour every input by the network’s answer.
pullback.c3: The straight line in hidden space becomes a curved band in the input plane. That non-linear boundary is what a single neuron could never draw.

exam.title: The exam version
exam.c1: Exams often want the weights by hand with step activations. One standard answer: h₁ = OR, h₂ = NAND, output = AND.
exam.c2: Check the table row by row: only (0,1) and (1,0) make both hidden units fire.
exam.c3: And a classic trap: stack linear layers and you get W₂W₁x — still one linear function, still one line. The non-linearity is the whole point.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to remember for the exam.
recap.c2: Next: try the XOR page, where you can train this network with backpropagation step by step.

recap.1: One neuron = one straight line. XOR’s four inequalities contradict each other.
recap.2: A hidden layer moves the points: linear map, then a non-linear squash.
recap.3: In hidden space one line separates them; pulled back, it is a curved boundary.

points.1: Prove “a single perceptron cannot learn XOR” with the four inequalities: b < 0, w₁ + b > 0, w₂ + b > 0, w₁ + w₂ + b < 0.
points.2: Two hidden neurons are enough. A common hand answer is OR and NAND feeding an AND.
points.3: Without a non-linear activation, any number of layers collapses into one linear layer.
points.4: “Make the points linearly separable after the first layer” — sketch the hidden-space picture to show it.

exam.q: Network A is a single perceptron, Network B adds one hidden layer with two neurons. Show that A cannot learn XOR, and give weights with which B can.
exam.a: A: (0,0)→0 needs b < 0; (0,1), (1,0)→1 need w₂ + b > 0 and w₁ + b > 0, so w₁ + w₂ > −2b; (1,1)→0 needs w₁ + w₂ < −b < −2b. Contradiction. B (step units): h₁ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 0.5), h₂ = step(−x₁ − x₂ + 1.5), y = step(h₁ + h₂ − 1) with output 1 only when the sum is > 0.

bayes.title: A 99% accurate test — and you are probably fine
bayes.sub: Count 10,000 people and Bayes’ rule stops being a formula. Then see why one zero breaks naive Bayes, and how Laplace fixes it.

label.positive_q: You test positive. How likely is it that you have the virus?
label.false_alarms: The false alarms outnumber the real cases fifty to one.
label.not_99: A positive result means about a 2% chance — not 99%.
label.num_is: numerator = the {{n}} infected people who test positive
label.den_is: denominator = all {{n}} people who test positive
label.test_again: Test positive again: yesterday’s answer becomes today’s prior.
label.posterior_prior: Each positive result multiplies the odds by 0.99 / 0.05 ≈ 20.
label.argmax: To classify you only compare the two products — the shared denominator never changes the winner.
label.zero_kills: One count of zero makes the whole product zero.
label.no_low: No patient with Z = No had low blood pressure, so P(Low | No) = 0 / 5 — and the other three symptoms no longer matter.
label.alpha_note: α = 1: pretend every value was seen once more. m = number of values the feature can take.
label.all_evidence: Now every symptom counts again, and no class is ruled out by one missing combination.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: This is the example from lecture 2, and some version of it appears in almost every paper.

question.title: The question
question.c1: One person in a thousand carries a virus.
question.c2: The test catches 99% of infected people, and clears 95% of healthy people.
question.c3: You test positive. Most people guess 99%, or maybe 95%.
question.ponder: Make your own guess before we count. What is the chance you are infected?

crowd.title: Count people, not percentages
crowd.c1: Forget percentages for a moment. Picture 10,000 people.
crowd.c2: 0.1% of them — just 10 people — have the virus.

test.title: Everyone takes the test
test.c2: The 10 infected people: 99% of 10 is 9.9, so about 10 positive results.
test.c3: The 9,990 healthy people: 5% of them get a false positive. That is about 500 people.
test.c4: The test is good. The problem is that there are so many more healthy people to make mistakes on.

gather.title: Only the positives
gather.c1: You tested positive, so you are one of these. Gather everyone with a positive result.
gather.c3: So your chance is 10 out of 510 — about 2%. The base rate, not the test, dominates.

formula.title: The same thing as Bayes’ rule
formula.c1: Bayes’ rule is exactly this counting, written with probabilities.
formula.c2: The numerator is the infected positives. The denominator is every positive — the total probability of a positive result.
formula.c3: Plug in the lecture’s numbers: 0.00099 over 0.05094, about 0.0194. Write the denominator out in full — that is where exam marks are.

again.title: Test again
again.c1: What if you take the test a second time, and it is positive again?
again.c2: Use 2% as the new prior. One more positive takes it to about 28%, a third to about 89%.
again.c3: That is the idea behind repeat testing — and a favourite follow-up question.

naive.title: Many pieces of evidence
naive.c1: Real problems have several symptoms. Lecture 2’s disease Z table has four.
naive.c2: Naive Bayes assumes the symptoms are independent given the class, so the likelihood is just a product.
naive.c3: Multiply prior and likelihoods for each class, straight from the counts in the table.
naive.c4: Z = No wins. Normalise only if the question asks for a probability.

zero.title: When one count is zero
zero.c1: Now change one symptom: this patient has low blood pressure.
zero.c2: In the training data, no patient with Z = No had low blood pressure.
zero.c3: So that factor is zero, and it wipes out the whole product — no matter what the other symptoms say.
zero.ponder: Without collecting more data, how could you stop one unseen combination from vetoing a class?

laplace.title: α-Laplace smoothing
laplace.c1: Pretend you saw every value α more times than you did.
laplace.c2: Add α on top, and m·α at the bottom, where m is how many values the feature can take: 3 for blood pressure, 2 for diabetes.
laplace.c3: Nothing is zero any more. Exams love to ask for exactly this table with α = 1.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then try the base-rate page, and the naive Bayes table with smoothing switched on.

recap.1: Turn percentages into counts out of 10,000: 10 true positives versus 500 false ones.
recap.2: P(V | +) = P(+ | V)P(V) / P(+), and P(+) adds both ways of testing positive.
recap.3: Naive Bayes multiplies likelihoods; one zero kills a class, so smooth with (count + α) / (N + mα).

points.1: Always write the denominator with the total-probability rule: P(+) = P(+ | V)P(V) + P(+ | H)P(H).
points.2: A positive result from a rare condition is usually a false alarm — expect an answer near 2%, not 99%.
points.3: For classification you may drop the denominator: compare P(B)·∏P(eⱼ | B) across classes.
points.4: Laplace smoothing adds α to every count and m·α to the class total; m is the number of values of that feature, not the number of features.

exam.source: Lecture 2 · asked in this form in 2022 Fall and 2022 Spring midterms
exam.q: 0.1% of a population carries a virus. The test is positive for 99% of carriers and negative for 95% of non-carriers. A patient tests positive. What is P(virus | +)?

backprop.title: Backpropagation by the numbers
backprop.sub: One forward pass, one error, and the chain rule run backwards through lecture 6’s XOR network — every number the final exam asks for.

label.edge_key: Edge colour: blue positive, red negative. Thickness = |weight|.
label.how_steep: how steep the sigmoid is at this point
label.how_much_input: how much signal came in along w₅
label.delta_k_is: The first two factors are reused for every weight into O: that product is δk.
label.blame: Blame flows back along the same edges, scaled by their weights.
label.old_w5: Use w₅ and w₆ from before this step’s update — the lecture does.
label.zero_input: With input (0, 0), the gradient for w₁…w₄ is zero: those weights cannot move this step. Only the θs change.
label.loss: loss ½(T − O)², mean of 4 samples
label.rate_title: The learning rate η decides the step size
label.rate_small: too small: creeps towards the bottom
label.rate_good: about right: lands in a few steps
label.rate_large: too large: overshoots and climbs out

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Every final asks you to push numbers through a small network and update its weights by hand. Let us do it once, slowly, and see why each factor is there.

setup.title: The network
setup.c1: This is lecture 6’s 2-2-1 network for XOR: six weights, three biases, all starting at the lecture’s values.
setup.c2: The learning rate is 0.5 and every neuron uses the sigmoid.

forward.title: Forward pass
forward.c1: Signals flow left to right. Each neuron adds up weight times input, adds θ, and applies the sigmoid.
forward.c2: With input (0, 0) both hidden sums are zero, and σ(0) is exactly 0.5.
forward.c4: We wanted 0. The error is E = ½(T − O)².

chain.title: The chain rule
chain.c1: To fix w₅ we need to know how E changes when w₅ changes. The chain rule splits that into three simpler questions.
chain.c2: How does E change with O? That is O − T: how wrong we are.
chain.c3: How does O change with its input z? For the sigmoid that is O(1 − O): the slope of the curve.
chain.c4: How does z change with w₅? By h₁, the signal travelling along w₅.
chain.c5: The first two factors do not depend on which weight we are fixing. Together they are δk = 0.107022.

update_out.title: Update the output weights
update_out.c1: The update rule: subtract η times δ times whatever flows into that weight.
update_out.c2: For w₅ that input is h₁ = 0.5: w₅ becomes 0.833244 (the lecture rounds δk first and prints 0.833245 — both get the mark).
update_out.c3: w₆ and θ₃ move the same way — θ’s input is always 1.

hidden.title: Blame the hidden neurons
hidden.c1: Hidden neurons have no target. Their share of the error comes back through the weights.
hidden.c2: Each δj multiplies δk by the weight it travelled along, then by the sigmoid slope h(1 − h).
hidden.c3: δj1 = 0.023008 and δj2 = −0.036922. h₂ fed the output through a negative weight, so its blame has the opposite sign.
hidden.c4: One exam detail: these deltas use w₅ and w₆ from before the update.

update_hidden.title: Update the hidden weights
update_hidden.c1: Same rule for the first layer: w ← w − η δj x.
update_hidden.c2: But this input is (0, 0). Every x is zero, so w₁ to w₄ do not change at all.
update_hidden.c3: Only the biases move. Over the next three samples the other weights get their turn.
update_hidden.ponder: If both hidden neurons started with identical weights, would they ever become different?

train.title: Repeat ten thousand times
train.c1: That was one step for one sample. An epoch runs all four samples; then repeat.
train.c2: The loss falls slowly at first, then quickly once the hidden layer finds a useful shape.
train.c3: After 10,000 epochs the network gives outputs close to 0, 1, 1, 0: XOR, learned.

rate.title: Choosing η
rate.c1: η scales every step. Here is the same descent on a simple bowl with three learning rates.
rate.c2: Too small and you creep towards the bottom.
rate.c3: About right and you land in a few steps.
rate.c4: Too large and each step overshoots further than the last. Exams ask exactly this trade-off.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three formulas cover every backprop question in this course.
recap.c2: Then open the XOR page and run these steps yourself, with Quiz mode on.

recap.1: Output: δk = (O − T)·O(1 − O). Hidden: δj = Oj(1 − Oj)·δk·wjk, using the old wjk.
recap.2: Update: w ← w − η·δ·(the input of that weight); a bias’s input is 1.
recap.3: Zero inputs give zero updates; η too large overshoots, too small crawls.

points.1: Write the course’s sign convention: δk = (O − T)·O(1 − O) and subtract. Mixing (T − O) with subtraction flips every update.
points.2: The hidden deltas use the weights before this sample’s update — say so if the paper is ambiguous.
points.3: A weight whose input is 0 does not change in that step; biases always change because their input is 1.
points.4: Step activations cannot be trained by backprop (zero gradient almost everywhere, Final 2024 Q4c).

exam.source: Lecture 6 example · Final 2024 Q4(d) asks the same steps on another network
exam.q: For the lecture’s XOR network (η = 0.5) and the first sample (0, 0) with T = 0: compute O, δk, and the new w₅.

cnn.title: From a sliding window to a CNN’s shape table
cnn.sub: Read the output-size formula straight off the animation, see why a kernel’s depth matches its input, and why CNNs need a hundredth of an MLP’s weights.

label.count_positions: How many places can a 3-wide window stand in a row of 7?
label.same: One ring of zeros keeps the size: Keras calls this padding="same".
label.stride3: stride 3: jump three cells at a time
label.never_seen: The last row and column are never covered — the lecture says the window “does not fit”.
label.depth_matches: a filter is as deep as its input
label.one_map: Each filter slides over the whole volume and produces one 32 × 32 map. Ten filters, ten maps.
label.same_job: Same input, same output shape: a convolution versus a dense layer
label.sharing: One small kernel is reused at every position (parameter sharing), and each output sees only a small window.
label.final22: Final 2022 Part B Q1 — shapes and parameters, layer by layer

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Every final has a table to fill in: the output shape and parameter count of each layer. All of it comes from one picture — a window sliding over an image.

slide.title: Slide, multiply, add
slide.c1: A 7 × 7 image and a 3 × 3 kernel. Put the kernel on the top-left corner.
slide.c2: Multiply each pair of numbers, add them up: that is one output value. Then slide one step and repeat.
slide.c3: When the window has visited every position it can, the output is complete — and it is smaller than the image.

size.title: Where the size comes from
size.c1: Look at a single row. A window of width 3 can start at positions 1 to 5 in a row of 7.
size.c2: So the output width is N − K + 1 = 5.
size.c3: Add padding P on both sides and jump S cells at a time, and you get the formula on every exam: ⌊(N − K + 2P) / S⌋ + 1.

padding.title: Padding
padding.c1: Put a ring of zeros around the image. Now the window can be centred on the edge pixels too.
padding.c2: With P = 1 and a 3 × 3 kernel, the output is 7 × 7 again — the same size as the input.

stride.title: Stride
stride.c1: Stride 3: the window jumps three cells at a time.
stride.c2: 7 − 3 = 4, and 4 / 3 is not a whole number. Round down: two positions, a 2 × 2 output.
stride.c3: The last row and column are never looked at. Exams floor the result; they call it “does not fit”.
stride.ponder: How much padding would make a 3 × 3 kernel with stride 3 fit a 7 × 7 image exactly?

channels.title: Depth and filters
channels.c1: Real images have channels. Lecture 8’s example: 32 × 32 × 3, ten 5 × 5 filters, stride 1, padding 2.
channels.c2: A filter always reaches through the full depth of its input, so each one is 5 × 5 × 3.
channels.c3: Each filter produces one 32 × 32 map. Ten filters give a 32 × 32 × 10 output.
channels.c4: Parameters: each filter has 5·5·3 weights plus one bias — 760 in total, whatever the image size.

sharing.title: Why CNNs are small
sharing.c1: A dense layer producing the same 32 × 32 × 10 output needs a weight for every input–output pair.
sharing.c2: That is over 31 million weights, against 760.
sharing.c3: The kernel is shared across positions and only looks locally. That is the whole reason CNNs scale to images.

stack.title: A whole network
stack.c1: Now a full stack from the 2022 final: 224 × 224 × 3 in, 1000 classes out.
stack.c2: Each layer’s shape comes from the same formula; pooling and global pooling have no parameters; only conv and dense layers do.
stack.c3: About two million parameters in total. Flatten the image into a dense layer instead and you need 150 million.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three rules fill in the whole shape table.
recap.c2: Then build your own stack on the CNN shapes page and check every number.

recap.1: Output size: ⌊(N − K + 2P) / S⌋ + 1. Padding “same” keeps N / S.
recap.2: Conv parameters: (K·K·C_in + 1) × filters — the image size does not matter.
recap.3: Pooling, flatten and dropout have no parameters; dense: (inputs + 1) × units.

points.1: Show the working for every layer: ⌊(N − K + 2P) / S⌋ + 1, then the parameter product. Marks are for the working.
points.2: A filter’s depth equals the input’s channel count. The number of filters becomes the output depth.
points.3: Explain the CNN–MLP gap with two phrases: parameter sharing and sparse (local) connections.
points.4: If (N − K + 2P) is not divisible by S, floor — the last pixels are skipped. The 2022 marking scheme slipped here (13 × 13 instead of 14 × 14).

exam.source: Lecture 8 all-in-one example · same format in Final 2022 B Q1 and Final 2023 Q6
exam.q: Input 32 × 32 × 3, ten 5 × 5 filters, stride 1, padding 2. What is the output shape, and how many parameters does the layer have?

kmeans.title: K-Means: two steps, repeated
kmeans.sub: Assign every point to its nearest centre, move each centre to its points’ mean, repeat. Watch why it always stops, why it can stop in the wrong place, and how the exam table is filled in.

label.no_labels: 36 points, no labels. Can we find the groups?
label.seeds: Start with k centres — here placed by hand, badly on purpose.
label.assign: Assign: every point joins its nearest centre.
label.update: Update: every centre moves to the mean of its points.
label.why_a: each point switches only to a closer centre, so its term can only shrink.
label.why_b: the mean is the point with the smallest total squared distance to the group.
label.why_stop: SSE never goes up, and there are only finitely many ways to split the points — so the loop must stop.
label.stuck: Two centres share one blob and one centre straddles two. No single step can improve it, so K-Means stops here.
label.restarts: That is a local minimum. In practice: run several times from different seeds and keep the lowest SSE.
label.medicine: Lecture 4: four medicines, k = 2, seeds A and B
label.table_done: Round 2 changes nobody’s cluster, so the algorithm stops.
label.elbow: The elbow: after k = 3 the SSE barely drops.
label.not_min: Do not pick the k with the smallest SSE — that is always k = n.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: K-Means appears in six of the nine past papers, almost always as a table you fill in round by round. Here is what that table is doing.

data.title: Points without labels
data.c1: Here are 36 points with no labels. We suspect there are groups.
data.c2: K-Means needs one number from us: k, how many groups to look for.
data.c3: Then it needs k starting centres. We place three deliberately badly, to watch the algorithm recover.

steps.title: The two steps
steps.c1: Step A, assign: measure the distance from each point to every centre, and give the point the colour of the nearest one.
steps.c2: The coloured regions show which centre is nearest everywhere on the plane.
steps.c3: Step B, update: move each centre to the average position of the points it just won.
steps.c4: That average is all the update step ever does.

iterate.title: Repeat until nothing changes
iterate.c1: Now repeat: assign, update, assign, update.
iterate.c2: Watch the SSE bars: the total squared distance from points to their centres, after each round.
iterate.c3: In the last round no point changes cluster. Then the centres cannot move again — that is convergence.
iterate.ponder: Will the SSE ever go up from one round to the next? Why, or why not?

why.title: Why it always stops
why.c1: Everything K-Means does lowers one number, the SSE.
why.c2: The assign step only moves a point to a closer centre.
why.c3: The update step puts each centre at its group’s mean, the best place for squared distances.
why.c4: SSE never rises and there are finitely many partitions, so K-Means always converges — but not necessarily to the best answer.

local.title: Stuck in a local minimum
local.c1: Same points, three other starting centres.
local.c2: It converges — at an SSE more than three times worse.
local.c3: So “K-Means always converges” is true, but “to the optimal clustering” is false. A classic true/false question.

table.title: The exam table
table.c1: On paper it looks like this. Lecture 4: four medicines, k = 2, starting at A and B.
table.c2: Fill the distance table, take the nearest centre, then average each cluster to get the new centres.
table.c3: Round 2 uses the new centres. Same table, same steps.
table.c4: Nobody changed cluster, so we stop. The sentence the marking scheme wants: the cluster assignment no longer changes.

elbow.title: Choosing k
elbow.c1: k is not learned. To choose it, run K-Means for k = 1, 2, 3 … and plot the best SSE.
elbow.c2: The curve falls steeply, then flattens. The bend — the elbow — is the k to choose.
elbow.c3: Never choose the smallest SSE: k = n puts each point in its own cluster with SSE zero.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then fill in a table yourself on the K-Means by hand page, with Quiz mode on.

recap.1: Assign to the nearest centre, move each centre to its cluster mean, repeat until no point changes.
recap.2: SSE never increases, so it always converges — but possibly to a local minimum that depends on the seeds.
recap.3: Choose k with the elbow method, not the smallest SSE.

points.1: Show the full distance table every round, then the new centres as means. Use the distance the question names (some papers want squared distance).
points.2: Ties go to the lower-numbered centre unless the paper says otherwise — write your rule down.
points.3: Stop only after a full round in which no point changes cluster; that sentence earns the mark.
points.4: True/false favourites: it always converges (true); it finds the global optimum (false); a cluster can end up empty (true).

exam.source: Lecture 4 practice · same format in the 2022 Fall, 2022 Spring, 2023 Fall, 2023 Spring and 2025 Spring midterms
exam.q: Medicines A(1,1), B(2,1), C(4,3), D(5,4). Run K-Means with k = 2, starting centres A and B, Euclidean distance. Give the clusters and centres after it converges.
exam.a: Round 1: A → C1; B, C, D → C2. New centres C1 = (1, 1), C2 = (3.67, 2.67). Round 2: A, B → C1; C, D → C2. New centres C1 = (1.5, 1), C2 = (4.5, 3.5). Round 3: no change, so stop: {A, B} and {C, D}.

alphabeta.title: Alpha-beta: skipping what cannot matter
alphabeta.sub: Minimax looks at every leaf. Alpha-beta proves that some leaves cannot change the answer, and never looks at them.

label.bubble: Fill in from the bottom: each MAX node takes the largest child value, each MIN node the smallest.
label.cut: Cut at {{node}}: α = {{a}} ≥ β = {{b}} — skip {{n}} child
label.why_1: The root (MAX) can already get {{a}} through B.
label.why_2: C is a MIN node. After seeing F = 2, C is worth at most 2, whatever G holds.
label.why_3: MAX will never choose a move worth ≤ 2 over one worth 7. So G cannot matter.
label.order_note: Pruning never changes the answer, only how much work it takes. Best moves first prune the most.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Every final asks you to run alpha-beta by hand: which nodes get pruned, and what are α and β along the way. Let us watch it happen.

tree.title: A game tree
tree.c1: Two players take turns. MAX wants the score high, MIN wants it low.
tree.c2: Triangles pointing up are MAX’s turns, pointing down are MIN’s.
tree.c3: The leaves are scores of finished positions, from MAX’s point of view.

minimax.title: Minimax
minimax.c1: Minimax fills the tree from the bottom up.
minimax.c2: Each MAX node takes the largest child value; each MIN node the smallest.
minimax.c3: The root gets 7: with best play from both sides, that is the score.
minimax.ponder: Minimax looked at all 8 leaves. Can you spot one whose value cannot possibly change the answer?

search.title: Alpha-beta, step by step
search.c1: Alpha-beta searches the same tree depth-first, left to right, carrying two numbers down.
search.c2: α is the best score MAX is already guaranteed on this path; β is the best MIN is guaranteed. They start at −∞ and +∞.
search.c3: At E, the first leaf is 8. E is a MAX node, so it is worth at least 8 — but B, above it, already has 7 and will take the smaller. α ≥ β: skip E’s second leaf.
search.c4: B returns 7, so the root’s α becomes 7. Now C: its first child F is worth only 2.
search.c5: C is a MIN node, so it is worth at most 2. α = 7 ≥ β = 2: the whole subtree G is cut. Only 5 of 8 leaves were evaluated.

why.title: Why the cut is safe
why.c1: Look at the second cut more slowly.
why.c2: The root can already guarantee 7 by moving to B.
why.c3: C is a MIN node that has found 2, so its value is at most 2, whatever G contains.
why.c4: MAX will never pick C. Whatever is under G, the root value stays 7. That is the rule: cut when α ≥ β.

order.title: Move order matters
order.c1: With this order, alpha-beta evaluated 5 leaves.
order.c2: Rearrange the same eight values badly and it has to look at all 8 — but the answer is still 7.
order.c3: So pruning saves work without changing the result, and checking the best moves first saves the most.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then run your own leaf values on the alpha-beta page, step by step.

recap.1: Minimax: MAX nodes take the largest child, MIN nodes the smallest, filled from the leaves up.
recap.2: Alpha-beta passes α (MAX’s guarantee) and β (MIN’s guarantee) down, and cuts the remaining children when α ≥ β.
recap.3: Pruning never changes the root value; good move order prunes more.

points.1: Write α and β at every node you enter, in the order you enter them — that is what the marking scheme checks.
points.2: At a MAX node update α; at a MIN node update β; cut the remaining children as soon as α ≥ β.
points.3: Mark pruned branches clearly, including whole subtrees, not just single leaves.
points.4: True/false: alpha-beta returns the same root value as minimax (true); it always prunes something (false — order matters).

exam.source: Lecture 10 · the same task appears in the 2022, 2023 and 2024 finals
exam.q: For the tree MAX( MIN( MAX(6,7), MAX(8,9) ), MIN( MAX(1,2), MAX(0,4) ) ), run alpha-beta left to right. Which leaves are never evaluated, and what is the root value?
exam.a: D = 7 so B’s β = 7. At E the first leaf 8 gives α = 8 ≥ β = 7: the leaf 9 is pruned. B = 7, root α = 7. At C, F = 2 gives β = 2 ≤ α = 7: the whole subtree MAX(0,4) is pruned. Root value 7; leaves 9, 0 and 4 are never evaluated.

knn.title: K nearest neighbours, and why units matter
knn.sub: Classify a new customer by asking the closest ones. Then watch standardization turn an ellipse into a circle — and change who counts as “closest”.

label.new_customer: A new customer: 161 cm, 61 kg. Which size?
label.no_training: KNN has no training step. It just keeps the data and compares.
label.fifth_changed: The 5th-nearest neighbour changes: (160, 64) is replaced by (165, 61).
label.still_m: Here the vote is still 4 M : 1 L, but in general standardizing can change the answer.
label.k1: k = 1 follows every single point: a jagged boundary that memorises noise (overfitting).
label.choose_k: Choose k with validation data — and an odd k for two classes, so votes cannot tie.
label.k15: k = 15 asks almost everyone: the majority size (L) takes the whole plane — even the M customers are now predicted L (underfitting).

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: KNN shows up in seven of the nine papers: compute distances, pick the k closest, vote — and standardize first.

data.title: The data
data.c1: Lecture 3: eighteen customers, their height, weight and T-shirt size.
data.c2: A new customer arrives: 161 cm, 61 kg. We have to guess the size.
data.c3: KNN does not build a model in advance. It only needs the data and a distance.

distance.title: Measure every distance
distance.c1: Measure the straight-line distance from the new customer to every stored customer.
distance.c2: Sort them. The closest is (160, 60), only 1.41 away.

vote.title: Take a vote
vote.c1: With k = 1 we copy the single closest customer: M.
vote.c2: With k = 3, three neighbours vote. With k = 5, the lecture’s choice, the vote is 4 M against 1 L.
vote.c3: Here every k says M. The neighbourhood is mostly medium.
vote.c4: The yellow ring is the radius that just reaches the k-th neighbour.
vote.ponder: With two classes, why do people prefer an odd k?

scale.title: Standardize first
scale.c1: Height is in centimetres and weight in kilograms. Which one matters more in the distance depends only on the units.
scale.c2: The fix is to measure each feature in standard deviations: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation.
scale.c3: Watch the plane stretch: height spreads 4.33 cm per unit, weight 2.63 kg per unit.
scale.c4: In the new units the neighbourhood is a circle again — and the fifth neighbour is a different customer.
scale.c5: Exams give you the mean and standard deviation. Standardize the test point with the training statistics too.

boundary.title: What k does to the boundary
boundary.c1: Colour every point of the plane by its prediction. With k = 1 the boundary follows every single customer.
boundary.c2: With k = 15 it smooths out so much that the majority class takes over: less sensitive to one odd point, but blind to real structure.
boundary.c3: Small k overfits, large k underfits. Pick k with validation data.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then move the test point yourself on the KNN page, with standardization on and off.

recap.1: Compute the distance to every training point, take the k closest, majority vote.
recap.2: Standardize each feature with (x − mean) / std of the training data before measuring distance.
recap.3: Small k overfits, large k underfits; use an odd k for two classes.

points.1: Write the full distance table, sorted, and mark the k nearest before you vote.
points.2: Standardize with the training mean and standard deviation — and apply the same numbers to the test point.
points.3: KNN has no training phase but prediction is expensive: every query compares against every stored point.
points.4: Odd k avoids ties with two classes; say how you break a tie if k is even.

exam.source: Lecture 3 T-shirt example · KNN appears in the 2022–2025 midterms and Final 2022
exam.q: Training means: height 164, weight 62.33; standard deviations 4.33 and 2.63. Standardize the test customer (161 cm, 61 kg).
exam.a: z_height = (161 − 164) / 4.33 ≈ −0.69; z_weight = (61 − 62.33) / 2.63 ≈ −0.51. Use these, with the training points standardized the same way, to compute distances.

perceptron.title: The perceptron learning rule
perceptron.sub: One neuron is one straight line. Watch the learning rule nudge that line one mistake at a time — and see why it never settles on XOR.

label.step: The step activation outputs 1 on one side of a line and 0 on the other.
label.line: All points with z = 0 form a straight line: the decision boundary.
label.normal: The weight vector w points straight across the line, towards the side that outputs 1.
label.theta_shift: Turning w turns the line; changing θ slides it without turning.
label.case_ok: Correct: the error is 0, so nothing changes.
label.case_up: Should have fired: add η·x to w. The line turns towards including x.
label.case_down: Fired wrongly: subtract η·x. The line turns away from x.
label.only_mistakes: Only mistakes move the line. A whole epoch without a mistake means it has converged.
label.cols: ep │ x  T │ z → O │ new w, θ
label.updated: Mistake (T − O = {{d}}): w and θ move.
label.xor: XOR: four points no line can split
label.never: The weights cycle for ever. No straight line exists, so the rule never stops.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Four midterms ask you to fill in a perceptron table by hand. Here is the picture behind every row of it.

neuron.title: One artificial neuron
neuron.c1: Inputs come in, each multiplied by a weight. The neuron adds them up, plus a bias θ.
neuron.c2: Then a step function: output 1 if the sum is at least 0, otherwise 0.
neuron.c3: So the whole neuron is a yes/no decision about which side of a line a point is on.

geometry.title: Weights draw a line
geometry.c1: Set z to zero and you get a line: w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + θ = 0.
geometry.c2: The weight vector points across the line, towards the side that outputs 1. Turn w and the line turns with it.
geometry.c3: θ slides the line back and forth without turning it.

rule.title: The learning rule
rule.c1: The perceptron learns from one sample at a time: Δw = η(T − O)x, Δθ = η(T − O).
rule.c2: If the output is right, T − O = 0 and nothing moves.
rule.c3: If it should have fired but did not, x is added to w: the line swings towards including that point.
rule.c4: If it fired but should not have, x is subtracted: the line swings away.
rule.ponder: If a sample sits at x = (0, 0), which part of the neuron can the rule still change?

run.title: Learning AND, row by row
run.c1: Lecture 5’s example: learn AND, starting from w = (0.1, 0.5), θ = −0.8, η = 0.2.
run.c2: Each row: compute z, compare O with T, and update only when they differ. The dashed line is where the boundary was before the update.
run.c3: Watch the shaded side shrink until only (1, 1) is inside it.
run.c4: One full epoch with no mistakes: the perceptron has converged.

xor.title: XOR never settles
xor.c1: Now XOR. No straight line separates its classes.
xor.c2: Every epoch still has mistakes, and every mistake drags the line somewhere else.
xor.c3: The perceptron convergence theorem only promises to stop when a separating line exists. For XOR you need a hidden layer.

traps.title: Exam traps
traps.c1: Three details decide whether your table gets full marks.
traps.c2: First: is the step “z ≥ 0” or “z > 0”? Papers differ, and rows that land exactly on z = 0 flip.
traps.c3: Second: with outputs ±1 a mistake gives T − O = ±2, so every update doubles.
traps.c4: Third: converged means a whole epoch without an update — not one correct row.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then fill in the perceptron table yourself, with Quiz mode on.

trap.1: Check the activation: lecture 5 fires when z ≥ 0, 2022 Fall only when z > 0.
trap.2: With ±1 outputs, T − O = ±2 — the step is twice as big as with 0/1 outputs.
trap.3: Stop only after a complete epoch with no update.

recap.1: A perceptron is one line: w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + θ = 0, with w pointing to the side that outputs 1.
recap.2: Update only on mistakes: Δw = η(T − O)x, Δθ = η(T − O).
recap.3: It converges exactly when the data are linearly separable; XOR never converges.

points.1: Write every row: x, T, z, O, then Δw and the new w and θ — even when nothing changes.
points.2: Read the activation definition carefully (≥ or >, 0/1 or ±1) before the first row.
points.3: The bias θ is updated like a weight whose input is always 1.
points.4: Answer “has it converged?” with the epoch rule: a whole pass with no update.

exam.source: Lecture 5 AND example · tables in the 2022 Fall, 2022 Spring, 2023 Fall and 2023 Spring midterms
exam.q: w = (0.1, 0.5), θ = −0.8, η = 0.2, f(z) = 1 if z ≥ 0 else 0. Process the AND sample (0, 1) with T = 0. What are O and the new weights?

evaluate.title: Is the model actually good?
evaluate.sub: Why 95% accuracy can mean a useless model, how the confusion matrix splits right and wrong, and how unshuffled cross-validation can score 0%.

label.lazy_model: 100 patients, 5 of them sick. A model that always answers “healthy”:
label.patients: {{n}} patients, sorted by what they really have (rows) and what the model said (columns).
label.diag: The diagonal is right; the other two cells are the two kinds of mistake.
label.precision_q: Of everyone the model flagged, how many really were sick?
label.recall_q: Of everyone who really was sick, how many did the model find?
label.harmonic: the harmonic mean of precision P and recall R
label.f1_punish: If either P or R is small, F1 is small. The ordinary average would hide it.
label.cv_setup: 80 samples, 4 classes × 20, kept sorted by class. 2-fold cross-validation:
label.unseen: Each test fold contains only classes the training fold has never seen: every prediction is wrong.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: A number like “95% accurate” sounds good. Lecture 3 and several papers ask you to look behind it.

lazy.title: The 95% model
lazy.c1: A hundred patients; five are sick.
lazy.c2: A model that simply says “healthy” to everyone is right 95 times out of 100.
lazy.c3: And it found none of the sick patients. Accuracy alone can hide that.
lazy.ponder: What single number would expose this model immediately?

matrix.title: The confusion matrix
matrix.c1: Lecture 3’s disease example: 126 patients, 20 of them sick.
matrix.c2: Sort every patient into a cell: what they really have, against what the model said.
matrix.c3: True positives and true negatives on the diagonal; false negatives and false positives off it.
matrix.c4: Accuracy is the diagonal over everything: 81%. Still looks fine.

pr.title: Precision and recall
pr.c1: Now look at one class at a time — here, “sick”.
pr.c2: Precision reads down the predicted-yes column: of the 8 flagged patients, only 2 are sick. 25%.
pr.c3: Recall reads across the actual-yes row: of the 20 sick patients, the model found 2. 10%.
pr.c4: Precision asks “can I trust a yes?”, recall asks “did I miss anyone?”.

f1.title: F1
f1.c1: F1 combines them with the harmonic mean.
f1.c2: Precision 1 with recall 0.02 averages to about one half, but F1 is about 0.04.
f1.c3: So a high F1 needs both numbers to be high. For our model F1 is 0.14 — it exposes what 81% accuracy hid.

cv.title: The cross-validation trap
cv.c1: D-fold cross-validation cuts the data into D parts; each part is the test set once.
cv.c2: But if the data are sorted by class and never shuffled, the first test fold holds classes 0 and 1 — and training sees only 2 and 3.
cv.c3: Swap the folds: the same thing happens. Every test sample is a class the model never saw: 0% accuracy.
cv.c4: Shuffle first and every fold contains every class.
cv.c5: Stratified folds guarantee it: each class is dealt evenly into every fold.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then build your own confusion matrix and folds on the practice pages.

recap.1: Accuracy hides imbalance: always look at the confusion matrix.
recap.2: Precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / (TP + FN), F1 = 2PR / (P + R).
recap.3: Shuffle (or stratify) before D-fold cross-validation, or whole classes go missing from training.

points.1: Label the matrix axes before computing: rows actual, columns predicted (or the other way — papers differ).
points.2: Precision divides by a column (everything predicted positive); recall divides by a row (everything actually positive).
points.3: For multi-class F1 compute per class first, then macro (plain mean) or weighted (by support).
points.4: The unshuffled-folds question assumes a sample is correct only if its class appears in training — state that assumption.

exam.source: Pattern of 2023 Fall Q7, 2024 Spring Q7 and Final 2024 Q3(b)
exam.q: 80 samples, 4 classes with 20 each, sorted by class and not shuffled, are split into 2 folds for cross-validation. If a sample is classified correctly only when its class appears in the training fold, what is the mean accuracy? How do you fix it?
exam.a: Fold 1 holds classes 0 and 1, fold 2 holds classes 2 and 3. Each test fold’s classes are absent from its training fold, so both folds score 0%: mean 0%. Shuffle the data (or stratify the folds) before splitting; then every fold sees every class.

broadcast.title: Broadcasting, and pairwise distances in one line
broadcast.sub: Why (3, 1) + (1, 4) gives (3, 4), why (2, 3) + (2,) fails, and how one line of NumPy computes every distance between two sets of points.

label.shape: An array is a grid of numbers. Its shape lists the length of each axis.
label.elementwise: Arithmetic works element by element — as long as NumPy can line the shapes up.
label.pair_up: Same shape: each cell meets the cell in the same position.
label.rule: Different shapes: compare axes from the right. Equal, or one of them 1.
label.right_align: A length-1 axis is copied (stretched) to match the other — without using extra memory.
label.mismatch: The last axes are 3 and 2: neither is 1, so NumPy raises a ValueError.
label.fixed: b[:, None] turns b into a column (2, 1). Now axis −1 is 3 vs 1: stretch it.
label.no_loops: Every test point minus every training point, squared, summed over the coordinate axis — no Python loops.
label.memory: The expanded form never builds the (n, m, d) array: it needs only (n, m) memory.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Every midterm has a NumPy question, and most of them come down to one idea: broadcasting.

shape.title: Shapes
shape.c1: This array has 2 rows and 3 columns: shape (2, 3).
shape.c2: Axis 0 runs down the rows, axis 1 across the columns.
shape.c3: Arithmetic on arrays is element by element.

same.title: Same shape
same.c1: When the shapes match, each element pairs with the element in the same place.

stretch.title: The broadcasting rule
stretch.c1: Now a column of shape (3, 1) and a row of shape (1, 4).
stretch.c2: Line the shapes up from the right and compare each axis: they must be equal, or one of them must be 1.
stretch.c3: Each length-1 axis is stretched: the column copies itself sideways, the row copies itself downwards.
stretch.c4: Now both are (3, 4), and they add element by element.

mismatch.title: When it fails
mismatch.c1: A (2, 3) array plus a vector of length 2.
mismatch.c2: Align from the right: 3 against 2. Neither is 1 — ValueError.
mismatch.ponder: How could you change b so that each row of a gets its own number from b?

fix.title: The fix: add an axis
fix.c1: Insert a new axis: b[:, None] has shape (2, 1).
fix.c2: Now the last axis is 3 against 1, so b stretches across each row. Each row gets its own value.

pairwise.title: Pairwise distances in one line
pairwise.c1: The 2022 Spring midterm: distances from 2 test points to 4 training points.
pairwise.c2: Give the test points a middle axis and the training points a first axis: (2, 1, 2) and (1, 4, 2). Broadcasting produces every difference: (2, 4, 2).
pairwise.c3: Square and sum along the last axis — the coordinates — to get a (2, 4) table of squared distances.
pairwise.c4: Take the square root, and argsort each row to find the nearest neighbours.

expand.title: The memory-friendly version
expand.c2: Each term broadcasts to (2, 4): a column of test norms, a row of training norms, and a matrix product.
expand.c3: Same numbers, but no three-dimensional array in memory.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then try it in the NumPy playground, where every call shows its shapes.

recap.1: Compare shapes from the right: each axis must be equal or 1; length-1 axes stretch.
recap.2: Use None (np.newaxis) to add an axis so the shapes line up.
recap.3: Pairwise distances: X[:, None, :] − Y[None, :, :], square, sum over axis −1, square root.

points.1: Write the shapes at every step: (n, 1, d) − (1, m, d) → (n, m, d) → sum(axis=−1) → (n, m).
points.2: Summing over the wrong axis is the most common mistake — the coordinate axis is the last one.
points.3: If a question says “no loops”, broadcasting or the ‖x‖² + ‖y‖² − 2x·y expansion is expected.
points.4: A shape error question: align from the right and name the first axis that is neither equal nor 1.

exam.source: 2022 Spring midterm Q2(c) · broadcasting appears in every midterm 2022–2025
exam.q: X_train has shape (4, 2) and X_test has shape (2, 2). Write one line of NumPy that returns the (2, 4) matrix of Euclidean distances, and give the shape after each step.
exam.a: np.sqrt(((X_test[:, None, :] - X_train[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=-1)). Shapes: (2, 1, 2) − (1, 4, 2) → (2, 4, 2); squaring keeps (2, 4, 2); sum(axis=-1) → (2, 4); sqrt keeps (2, 4).

gaussian.title: Naive Bayes for continuous features
gaussian.sub: You cannot count how often “blood pressure = 66” happened. Fit a bell curve per class instead, read its height, and multiply as before.

label.continuous: An illustration: nine Z = Yes blood pressures with μ = 73, σ ≈ 6.2
label.count_zero: Nobody had exactly 66, so counting gives P(66 | Yes) = 0 — useless for continuous values.
label.per_class: One curve per class and per feature, using that class’s mean and standard deviation.
label.read_height: The likelihood is the height of each class’s curve at the observed value.
label.fever_far: 97 sits in the tail of the Yes curve but closer to the No curve’s peak.
label.mix: Gaussian likelihoods for BP and fever, counted likelihoods for diabetes and vomit — one product per class:
label.no_wins: Z = No wins, even though blood pressure alone pointed slightly towards Yes.
label.density: A density can be larger than 1 — it is not a probability. That is fine: we only compare classes.
label.which_sigma: COMP2211 papers define σ with n − 1 (2024 Spring midterm, Final 2024). Use the formula the paper prints.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Lecture 2 ends by asking: what if blood pressure and fever are numbers, not categories? Three papers have asked exactly that.

problem.title: Counting breaks
problem.c1: With categories we counted. But blood pressure is a number.
problem.c2: A new patient has blood pressure 66. In data like this, nobody has exactly 66.
problem.c3: Counting would give zero — and one zero wipes out the whole naive Bayes product.

bell.title: Fit a bell curve
bell.c1: Instead, assume the values in each class follow a Gaussian.
bell.c2: Its shape is fixed by two numbers from the training data: the mean μ…
bell.c4: We fit one such curve for every class and every continuous feature.

bp.title: Blood pressure = 66
bp.c1: Lecture 2’s numbers: for Z = Yes, μ = 73 and σ = 6.2; for Z = No, μ = 75 and σ = 7.9.
bp.c2: Draw a line at 66 and read where it meets each curve.
bp.c3: Those heights — 0.0340 for Yes, 0.0264 for No — replace the counted probabilities.

fever.title: Fever = 97
fever.c1: Fever: Yes is N(79, 10.2), No is N(86, 9.7).
fever.c2: At 97 the No curve is much higher: 0.0216 against 0.0082.
fever.c3: So fever pulls strongly towards No.

combine.title: Multiply as before
combine.c1: Now the usual naive Bayes product, mixing curve heights for numbers and counts for categories.
combine.c2: Prior, two Gaussian likelihoods, two counted likelihoods — for each class.
combine.c4: The class with the larger product wins: No.

density.title: Not a probability
density.c1: One more thing. Make σ small and watch the peak.
density.c2: The curve’s height climbs above 1. A density is not a probability; only the area under it is.
density.c3: That does not matter for naive Bayes: we only compare products between classes.
density.ponder: If one class has a much smaller σ, does that automatically make its likelihoods larger?

sigma.title: Which σ?
sigma.c1: Computing σ yourself? Check the divisor.
sigma.c2: With n − 1 these three temperatures give 0.656; dividing by n gives 0.535.
sigma.c3: COMP2211 papers print the n − 1 formula. Use it, and show the working.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then try the Gaussian naive Bayes page with your own data.

recap.1: For a continuous feature, replace counting with the Gaussian density f(x) of each class.
recap.2: Each class needs its own μ and σ per feature; the likelihood is the curve height at the observed value.
recap.3: Multiply with the prior and any counted likelihoods; compare classes — densities may exceed 1.

points.1: Write the Gaussian formula with the numbers substituted before giving the value — the substitution earns marks.
points.2: Compute μ and σ separately for each class, never over all the data.
points.3: Use the σ formula the paper gives; recent papers use the sample standard deviation (÷ n − 1).
points.4: Mixed features are fine: Gaussian for numeric features, counts (with smoothing) for categorical ones.

exam.source: Lecture 2 · continuous-feature questions in the 2023 Fall and 2024 Spring midterms and Final 2024
exam.q: For Z = Yes, blood pressure has μ = 73 and σ = 6.2. Compute the likelihood of blood pressure 66.

dilated.title: Dilated convolution, the way the final codes it
dilated.sub: A 3×3 kernel that sees a 5×5 area, the sizes you need for “same” padding, and the shift-and-add loop behind the six TODOs — checked against the paper’s printed output.

label.d1: Dilation 1: an ordinary 3×3 kernel. It sees a 3×3 patch.
label.d2: Dilation 2: the same 9 weights, spread out with gaps. Now they span 5×5.
label.paper_formula: The paper gives the ordinary size formula. Replace the kernel size with k_eff.
label.matches: This is exactly the output printed in the paper’s test script.
label.mask: Each entry survives with probability 1 − p; multiplying by the mask zeroes the rest.
label.why_dropout: Dropout stops neurons relying on any single input, which reduces overfitting.
label.test_time: It is used only during training. (Many libraries also divide by 1 − p; this question does not ask for it.)

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: The 2024 final introduced something the lectures only mention: dilated convolution. Here is the whole idea, then the code.

dilation.title: Spreading the kernel
dilation.c1: An ordinary 3×3 kernel reads a 3×3 patch.
dilation.c2: With dilation 2, leave one pixel between taps. Same nine weights, but they now cover a 5×5 area.
dilation.c3: That is the point: a wider view without more parameters.

formula.title: The sizes
formula.c1: The effective kernel size is d(k − 1) + 1: here 5.
formula.c2: “Same” padding needs d(k − 1)/2 zeros on each side: here 2.
formula.c3: Then the usual output formula, with k_eff instead of k: for the test, a 10×10 input with stride 2 gives 5×5.
formula.ponder: Before the next part: which padded rows does kernel row i read, for output rows 0, 1, 2, …?

shift.title: Shift and add
shift.c1: The given code does not slide the window. It loops over the nine kernel cells instead.
shift.c2: Kernel cell (i, j) reads rows i·d + r·S and columns j·d + c·S: one strided slice of the padded input.
shift.c3: Multiply that slice by kernel[i][j] and add it to the output. The test kernel has ones on its diagonal, so three slices add up.
shift.c4: After the third slice the output is exactly the matrix printed in the paper.

todos.title: Filling in the code
todos.c1: So the six blanks are: the padding, the two output sizes…
todos.c2: …the row and column indices for each kernel cell, with np.arange…
todos.c3: …and the accumulation: kernel[i, j] times the slice picked by those indices.
