dropout.title: Part (b): dropout
dropout.c1: Part (b) is one line: a random mask that keeps each value with probability 1 − p.
dropout.c2: np.random.rand gives uniform numbers in [0, 1); comparing with p gives True with probability 1 − p.
dropout.c3: Dropping random activations stops the network relying on any single one — regularisation.
dropout.c4: Only during training. At test time every neuron is used.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then revisit convolution and output sizes on the practice pages.

recap.1: Dilation spreads the kernel: k_eff = d(k − 1) + 1, same parameters, wider view.
recap.3: Shift-and-add: for each kernel cell, add kernel[i][j] × input[i·d + S·r, j·d + S·c].

points.1: Replace k by d(k − 1) + 1 everywhere the size formula uses the kernel size.
points.2: Check your formulas against the printed test output — 10×10, d = 2, S = 2, same padding must give 5×5.
points.3: The loop is over kernel cells, so each step adds a whole strided slice; build the indices with np.arange(output_size) * stride.
points.4: Dropout mask: np.random.rand(*shape) > p keeps each value with probability 1 − p.

exam.q: With a 3×3 kernel, dilation 2, stride 2 and “same” padding on a 10×10 input: what padding and what output size? Which padded rows does kernel row i = 1 read?
exam.a: pad = 2·(3 − 1)/2 = 2, so the padded input is 14×14. k_eff = 5, output = ⌊(14 − 5)/2⌋ + 1 = 5, i.e. 5×5. Kernel row 1 reads rows 1·2 + 2·r = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.

imagenp.title: Image processing without loops
imagenp.sub: A circular mask built by broadcasting two ranges, and a 3×3 blur done with one-dimensional np.convolve — the two tricks Final 2024 asked for.

label.broadcast_dist: A row of x-distances plus a column of y-distances broadcasts to the full distance grid — no loops.
label.boundary: “Boundary included” means ≤, not <. The comparison gives True/False, which multiplies as 1/0.
label.two_passes: A 3×3 mean filter is a horizontal 3-tap average followed by a vertical one.
label.cheaper: Two passes of 3 taps instead of 9 multiplications per pixel — and each pass is one-dimensional.
label.drop_pad: Outputs centred on a padding zero mix two rows: those are exactly the columns we cut off.
label.ones_note: Here v = [1, 1, 1] so you can check the sums; the exam uses v = [1/3, 1/3, 1/3].
label.edges_dark: Zero padding darkens the border: edge pixels average in zeros.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: The 2024 final asked for two image operations with no explicit loops. Both are broadcasting in disguise.

mask.title: (a) A circular mask
mask.c1: Keep the pixels within distance 100 of a centre, zero the rest.
mask.c2: np.arange gives every x and every y. Subtract the centre, and broadcast a row against a column: the distance of every pixel, at once.
mask.c3: Compare with the radius — boundary included, so ≤ — to get the mask.
mask.c4: Multiply the image by the mask. True counts as 1, False as 0.
mask.ponder: Why does y_dist need [:, None] but x_dist does not?

separable.title: (b) Split the blur
separable.c1: The 3×3 blur averages nine neighbours. But that matrix is an outer product of two thirds-vectors.
separable.c2: So blurring is a horizontal 3-tap average followed by a vertical one.
separable.c3: The question gives v = blur_filter.sum(0) for exactly this reason.

flatten.title: The flatten trick
flatten.c1: np.convolve only works on 1-D arrays. So pad every row with a zero at each end…
flatten.c2: …and flatten the whole image into one long strip.
flatten.c3: One convolution slides along the strip. Windows centred on a real pixel see its row neighbours — or a padding zero at the edge, which is exactly zero padding.
flatten.c4: Windows centred on a padding zero straddle two rows. Put one 0 back at each end, reshape, and cut off the first and last column: those bad values disappear.

result.title: Both directions
result.c2: Transpose, run the same function, transpose back: the vertical pass.
result.c3: The result is the 3×3 zero-padded mean blur, and the code has no loops.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then try broadcasting shapes yourself in the NumPy playground.

recap.1: Circle mask: dist = np.sqrt(x_dist ** 2 + y_dist[:, None] ** 2); img * (dist <= r).
recap.2: A 3×3 box blur = horizontal 3-tap pass, then the same on the transpose.
recap.3: Flatten trick: pad rows, flatten, np.convolve(…, 'valid'), pad the ends, reshape, drop the pad columns.

points.1: The broadcasting step is worth a mark on its own: one axis must be a column ([:, None]).
points.2: ≤ for “boundary included”; using < loses half a mark in the scheme.
points.3: After np.convolve(…, 'valid') the strip is two shorter — add the zeros back before reshaping.
points.4: Watch the paper’s example: np.convolve([1,2,3,4], [0,1,0.5], 'valid') is really [2.5, 4.0], not [2.5, 3.5] as printed.

exam.q: Write apply_circle_mask(img, center_x, center_y) for a 512×512 image and radius 100 (boundary included) without loops.
exam.a: indices = np.arange(512); x_dist = indices − center_x; y_dist = indices − center_y; dist = np.sqrt(x_dist ** 2 + y_dist[:, None] ** 2); img_masked = img * (dist <= 100).

otsu.title: Histograms and Otsu’s threshold
otsu.sub: Pour an image into its histogram, watch point operations reshape it, and let Otsu’s method find the threshold by itself — with Final 2024’s numbers.

label.sort_by_grey: A histogram forgets where pixels are and keeps only how bright they are.
label.same_shape: Contrast stretching keeps the shape and spreads it over 0…255.
label.binary: Thresholding keeps two values: 0 below T, 255 above.
label.which_T: Too low or too high and the coins merge with the table. Which T is right?
label.stable: One more round gives T = {{T}} again: stable.
label.flip_same: A flip moves pixels but changes no value: the histogram is identical.
label.point_vs: That is how Final 2024 Q5(a) expects you to recognise the flipped image.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Image processing questions in the finals keep coming back to one picture: the grey-level histogram.

hist.title: From image to histogram
hist.c1: Here is a small picture of coins on a table, 1,728 pixels.
hist.c2: Now let every pixel fall into the column for its brightness.
hist.c3: Two humps: the darker table and the brighter coins. Where the pixels were is gone; only how bright they are remains.

stretch.title: Point operations
stretch.c1: A point operation changes each pixel using only its own value — so you can see its effect on the histogram directly.
stretch.c2: Here the image is squeezed into grey levels 90 to 160. Contrast stretching maps the darkest to 0 and the brightest to 255.
stretch.c3: The histogram keeps its shape and spreads out.

threshold.title: Thresholding
threshold.c1: Thresholding turns every pixel into black or white: 255 if it is brighter than T, 0 otherwise.
threshold.c2: Slide T and watch the coins appear and disappear.
threshold.c3: The right T is somewhere between the two humps. Can we find it automatically?
threshold.ponder: If you had to choose T from the histogram alone, where would you put it — and why?

otsu.title: Otsu’s method
otsu.c1: Lecture 7’s Otsu method: start with T at the mean brightness.
otsu.c2: Split the pixels at T and average each side: μ1 for the dark side, μ2 for the bright side.
otsu.c3: Move T to the midpoint of the two means, then split again. Repeat until T stops moving.
otsu.c4: The final T falls between the humps, and the coins come out cleanly.

table.title: Final 2024 Q5(b)
table.c1: The exam version: this 3×3 image with T₀ = 100 and one iteration.
table.c2: Pixels ≤ 100 average to 21, pixels above to 128, so the new T is 74.5 — and the bottom row becomes 255.
table.c3: The advantage the marking scheme wants: T is chosen automatically, so the result is reproducible.

flip.title: Which transformation was it?
flip.c1: Another favourite: match images to their histograms.
flip.c2: Flipping the image moves pixels around without changing any value. The histogram stays exactly the same.
flip.c3: Stretching spreads it, thresholding leaves two bars, a flip changes nothing.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then try the histogram and Otsu page with your own images.

recap.1: A histogram counts pixels per grey level; it ignores position.
recap.2: Point operations act on each pixel’s value alone: stretching spreads the histogram, thresholding leaves two bars, a flip leaves it unchanged.
recap.3: Otsu: T₀ = mean (or given), T ← (μ1 + μ2)/2, repeat until stable.

points.1: Write μ1, μ2 and the new T for each iteration, and say which side a pixel equal to T goes to.
points.2: If the paper says “one iteration”, stop after one — do not run to convergence.
points.3: Advantages of Otsu: automatic and reproducible — two people get the same T.
points.4: Matching histograms: two bars → thresholding; same shape spread out → stretching; identical → flip.

exam.q: The 3×3 image [2 4 8 / 16 32 64 / 128 128 128] is thresholded with Otsu’s method from T = 100, one iteration. What is the new threshold and the resulting image?
exam.a: Pixels ≤ 100: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 → μ1 = 21. Pixels > 100: 128 × 3 → μ2 = 128. New T = (21 + 128)/2 = 74.5. Result: the first two rows become 0 and the bottom row 255.

affine.title: One matrix moves every pixel
affine.sub: Translation, reflection and rotation as lecture 7’s 2 × 3 matrix — what they keep, why a 3 × 3 kernel cannot flip, and which flips are safe augmentations.

label.y_down: x counts columns to the right, y counts rows downward, (0, 0) is the top-left pixel.
label.the_one: The extra 1 is what lets a matrix also shift.
label.last_column: (tx, ty) sits in the last column — the column the 1 multiplies.
label.ccw: y points down, so a positive θ turns counter-clockwise on screen.
label.may: “An affine transformation may preserve distances and angles” — TRUE (Final 2024 Q1(f)).
label.kernel_reach: A 3 × 3 kernel reaches one pixel. The corner pixel needs a value {{n}} pixels away.
label.sixty_three: On a 64 × 64 image: up to 63 pixels. No 3 × 3 kernel can flip it (Final 2024 Q5(e)).
label.aug_q: Which augmentation helps cats vs dogs but not handwritten digits?
label.aug_answer: Final 2022: a horizontal flip. Rotations and reflections earn the marks.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Translate, flip, rotate: lecture 7 does all of them with one 2 × 3 matrix. Here is why that works, and what the finals ask about it.

coords.title: Pixel coordinates
coords.c1: First, the coordinates. x counts columns to the right, y counts rows downward, and (0, 0) is the top-left pixel.
coords.c2: So “up” on screen means a smaller y. Keep that in mind — it decides which way a rotation turns.
coords.c3: Every transform in the lecture has the same shape: multiply [x, y, 1] by a 2 × 3 matrix M. The extra 1 is what lets a matrix also shift.

translate.title: Translation
translate.c1: Translation adds tx to every x and ty to every y.
translate.c2: In M that is the identity on the left and (tx, ty) in the last column — the column the 1 multiplies.
translate.c3: cv2.warpAffine fills the pixels nothing moved into with 0.

reflect.title: Reflection
reflect.c1: Reflection along the x-axis. Step one: y becomes −y, so the picture flips over row 0 and lands above the frame.
reflect.c2: Step two: add rows − 1 to slide it back in. The top row and the bottom row have swapped.
reflect.c3: So “reflect along the x-axis” turns the picture upside down: M = [[1, 0, 0], [0, −1, rows − 1]].
reflect.c4: Before we go on: which matrix mirrors the picture left to right instead?
reflect.ponder: Which 2 × 3 matrix mirrors the picture left to right? Write it down before you continue.

rotate.title: Rotation about the centre
rotate.c1: Answer: x becomes −x + (cols − 1), so M = [[−1, 0, cols − 1], [0, 1, 0]] — reflection along the y-axis.
rotate.c2: Rotation about the centre is three moves. First shift the centre to the origin…
rotate.c3: …then rotate about the origin. With y pointing down, a positive angle turns counter-clockwise on screen…
rotate.c4: …and shift back. Multiply the three and you get exactly the lecture’s matrix — the one cv2.getRotationMatrix2D returns.

survive.title: What survives?
survive.c1: What does an affine map keep? Watch a grid and a right triangle. A rotation keeps every length and every angle.
survive.c2: A shear keeps lines straight and parallel lines parallel, but lengths and angles change.
survive.c3: Uniform scaling keeps the angles but not the lengths.
survive.c4: Parallel lines and midpoints survive every affine map; distances and angles only some of them. So “may preserve distances and angles” is true.

global.title: Point, local or global?
global.c1: Is a flip a point operation? Each output pixel copies its value from somewhere else, so no — that is why Final 2022’s statement is false.
global.c2: Is it at least local? A 3 × 3 kernel only reaches one pixel away, but the edge pixels of a flip need values from the far side.
global.c3: On a 64 × 64 image that is up to 63 pixels, so no 3 × 3 kernel can flip it. And since no value changes, the histogram stays the same.

augment.title: Augmentation
augment.c1: Flips and rotations are also the classic data augmentations. Mirror a cat: still a cat.
augment.c2: Mirror a handwritten 2: not a digit any more. That is the Final 2022 answer — a horizontal flip helps cats vs dogs, not digits.
augment.c3: Rotate a 6 by 180° and it reads as a 9. An augmentation must never change the label.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.
recap.c2: Then try every transform yourself on the practice page.

recap.1: Every transform is [x′, y′] = M · [x, y, 1]; the last column shifts. In image coordinates y points down.
recap.2: Reflecting along the x-axis turns the image upside down: y′ = −y + (rows − 1). Rotation = shift, rotate, shift back.
recap.3: Affine maps keep parallel lines, not always distances or angles; they are not point operations, and a flip is global.

points.1: Write M as a 2 × 3 matrix acting on [x, y, 1]: the left 2 × 2 block turns, mirrors or scales; the last column shifts.
points.2: Reflections need the shift: x′ = −x + (cols − 1) or y′ = −y + (rows − 1), so corners land on corners.
points.3: T/F favourites: affine transforms are not point operations (Final 2022 F); they may preserve distances and angles (Final 2024 T).
points.4: Augmentation: a horizontal flip suits cats vs dogs but not digits (Final 2022) — rotations and reflections earn the marks.

exam.q: Is it possible to design a 3 × 3 kernel and apply convolution with it to flip a 64 × 64 image horizontally or vertically? If yes, give such a kernel. If not, explain why.
exam.a: No. Flipping is a global operation: the output pixel in column x takes the input pixel in column 63 − x, up to 63 pixels away. A 3 × 3 convolution is local — every output sees only its 3 × 3 neighbourhood, with the same weights everywhere — so it cannot reach that far.

ethics.title: AI ethics for the final
ethics.sub: The three areas a company must cover, how the EU’s seven principles map onto five common grounds, and six ways unfairness gets into a model.

label.areas_q: From which areas should an organisation make sure its AI models in production behave ethically?
label.areas_mark: Final 2024 Problem 9: one point for each area.
label.match_q: Lecture 11 practice: match each EU principle to a common ground.
label.surprise: The two to remember: privacy (C) and accountability (G) both go to autonomy.
label.loop_note: Each turn of the loop makes the data look more convincing, though nothing about the world has changed.
label.moral_q: What would a machine need in order to act as a moral agent?
label.trolley: The self-driving-car dilemma is a metaphor for hard trade-offs, not a realistic scenario.

1.name: Data ethics
1.what: Consent, privacy and secure handling; data that represents everyone fairly.

2.name: Model fairness
2.what: Models built so their decisions and recommendations are fair.

3.name: Monitoring and maintenance
3.what: Watch for model drift as incoming data changes; keep it working as intended.

human.name: Human bias
human.eg: Past hiring decisions train a hiring model, and it learns the old preferences.

loop.name: Feedback loops
loop.eg: Predictions decide where data is collected, so the data confirms the predictions.

sample.name: Sample size disparity
sample.eg: Fewer examples of a minority group make the model less accurate for that group.

unreliable.name: Unreliable data
unreliable.eg: Noisier data for some groups, e.g. an inaccurate census in some neighbourhoods.

proxy.name: Proxies
proxy.eg: Remove race, keep postcode — the model can still recover it.

culture.name: Cultural unawareness
culture.eg: A team that all looks alike may not notice who the system fails.

loop.1: Send police where the model predicts crime
loop.2: More patrols record more incidents there
loop.3: The new data shows more crime there
loop.4: The model predicts even more crime there

moral.4: The ability to work out the consequences of its own actions

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: The last question of every final is about ethics. It is short, it is definitional, and the marks are easy if you know the lists.

areas.title: Three areas
areas.c1: Final 2024 asked: in which areas must an organisation make sure its AI behaves ethically?
areas.c2: Data ethics: consent, privacy, secure handling, and data that represents people fairly.
areas.c3: Model fairness: building models whose decisions are fair.
areas.c4: Monitoring and maintenance: models drift as the data changes, so they must be watched and updated.

principles.title: Seven principles, five grounds
principles.c1: The EU lists seven principles for trustworthy AI.
principles.c2: The many lists of principles boil down to five common grounds: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice and explicability.
principles.c3: The lecture’s practice problem asks you to match them.
principles.ponder: Try it before the answer: which common ground does accountability (G) belong to?

match.title: The official matching
match.c1: Human agency, privacy and accountability go to autonomy. Robustness and safety to non-maleficence.
match.c2: Transparency to explicability, fairness to justice, well-being to beneficence.
match.c3: Written as the answer table: A1, B3, C1, D5, E4, F2, G1.

causes.title: Where unfairness comes from
causes.c1: Lecture 11 lists six causes of unfair models.
causes.c2: Human bias in the labels, and feedback loops where predictions shape the data.
causes.c3: Too few samples from a group, or less reliable data about it.
causes.c4: Proxy features that stand in for a removed sensitive attribute.
causes.c5: And blind spots in the team that builds the system.

loop.title: A feedback loop
loop.c1: Follow one loop around: the model sends patrols to a neighbourhood.
loop.c2: More patrols record more incidents there, and the new data seems to confirm the model.
loop.c3: So it predicts even more crime there — whatever the real rate is.

moral.title: Moral machines
moral.c1: Can a machine make moral decisions?
moral.c2: It would need beliefs about the world, intentions, moral knowledge, and the ability to compute the consequences of its actions.
moral.c3: The self-driving-car dilemma is a metaphor for the trade-offs autonomous systems face.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three lists to know by heart for the last question.

recap.1: Three areas: data ethics, model fairness, monitoring and maintenance.
recap.2: Five common grounds: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, explicability.
recap.3: Unfairness: human bias, feedback loops, sample size disparity, unreliable data, proxies, cultural unawareness.

points.1: Name the three areas exactly: data ethics, AI model fairness, AI model monitoring and maintenance.
points.2: Know the lecture’s matching table: A1, B3, C1, D5, E4, F2, G1.
points.3: For “why might a model be unfair”, give a cause and an example — e.g. proxies: postcode standing in for race.
points.4: Model drift is the reason monitoring matters: accuracy changes as incoming data changes.

exam.q: From what areas should organisations ensure the AI models they have in production function ethically?
exam.a: Data ethics (consent, privacy, unbiased and representative data); AI model fairness (fair decisions and recommendations); AI model monitoring and maintenance (watch for model drift and keep the model working as intended).

autograd.title: PyTorch: tensors and autograd
autograd.sub: A tensor is a NumPy array that remembers how it was made. Follow lecture 9’s example through the computational graph, call loss.backward(), and see where w.grad comes from.

label.tensor: A tensor is an n-dimensional array, like a NumPy array — with a device and gradient tracking.
label.cpu_ok: GPUs make training faster, but PyTorch trains and runs on the CPU too — a classic true/false trap.
label.recorded: Every operation on a tensor with requires_grad=True is recorded in the graph.
label.forward: Forward pass: numbers flow from x, w and b to the loss.
label.rows_same: The gradient for w_ij is the gradient at z_j times the input x_i that w_ij multiplied.
label.same_as_backprop: This is exactly lecture 6’s backpropagation — PyTorch just applies the chain rule for you.
label.inference: After training you only need the forward pass.
label.why_no_grad: torch.no_grad() stops recording the graph: less memory and faster inference.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Lecture 9 moves from hand-written NumPy networks to PyTorch. The key idea is that tensors remember how they were computed.

tensor.title: Tensors
tensor.c1: A tensor is an n-dimensional array, much like a NumPy array.
tensor.c2: It also has a dtype, a device — CPU or GPU — and a requires_grad flag.
tensor.c3: A GPU speeds up training, but it is not required: PyTorch also trains on the CPU. Converting to and from NumPy is one call.

graph.title: The computational graph
graph.c1: Lecture 9’s example: an input of ones, a target of zeros, and two parameters w and b that require gradients.
graph.c2: Each line of code adds a node to a graph: a matrix product, an addition, then the loss.
graph.c3: PyTorch records this graph as the code runs; nothing has to be declared in advance.

forward.title: Forward pass
forward.c1: Run the code and the numbers flow forward through the graph.
forward.c2: z = x·w + b gives three logits.
forward.c3: The loss compares σ(z) with the targets using binary cross-entropy, averaged over the three outputs.

backward.title: loss.backward()
backward.c1: Now call loss.backward(). Gradients flow backwards through the same graph.
backward.c2: At z each gradient is (σ(z_j) − y_j)/3.
backward.c3: They arrive at the leaves that require gradients: w.grad and b.grad. Look at w.grad — every row is the same.
backward.ponder: Why does every row of w.grad come out identical — exactly as in the lecture’s printed output?

rows.title: Why the rows match
rows.c1: By the chain rule, the gradient for w_ij is the gradient at z_j times x_i.
rows.c2: The input x is all ones, so every row of w.grad equals b.grad.
rows.c3: Nothing new: this is the backpropagation of lecture 6, done automatically.

nograd.title: Turning tracking off
nograd.c1: Once the model is trained you only need forward passes.
nograd.c2: Inside with torch.no_grad(), results have requires_grad = False.
nograd.c3: No graph is recorded, which saves memory and time at inference.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to take into the exam.

recap.1: A tensor is an n-d array with a dtype, a device (CPU or GPU) and optional gradient tracking.
recap.2: requires_grad=True records a graph; loss.backward() fills .grad by the chain rule.
recap.3: Use torch.no_grad() for inference; GPUs are faster but not required.

points.1: “Deep learning cannot run on a CPU” is false — GPUs are faster, not necessary.
points.2: Gradients are accumulated in .grad of leaf tensors with requires_grad=True.
points.3: autograd is backpropagation: the gradient of a weight is the downstream gradient times its input.
points.4: torch.no_grad() (or a model in evaluation) avoids recording the graph during inference.

exam.source: Lecture 9 example · the 2022 final’s true/false section asked about CPUs
exam.q: In lecture 9’s example x = torch.ones(5). After loss.backward(), why are all five rows of w.grad identical?
exam.a: ∂loss/∂w_ij = ∂loss/∂z_j · x_i. Every x_i is 1, so row i equals ∂loss/∂z = b.grad for every i.

drill.title: Concept check
drill.lead: Every final opens with ten true/false questions. These are original statements of the same kind, grouped by lecture. Answer, read why, and follow the link to the explainer or practice page.

np1.q: If a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4), then a[:, 1].shape is (3,).
np1.why: Indexing a column with a single integer removes that axis: three rows, one value each — a 1-D array of length 3. a[:, 1:2] would keep it as (3, 1).

np2.q: Adding an array of shape (4, 1) to one of shape (3,) gives shape (4, 3).
np2.why: Align from the right: (4, 1) and (1, 3). Each axis is equal or 1, so both stretch to (4, 3).

np3.q: Adding an array of shape (2, 3) to one of shape (2,) works by broadcasting.
np3.why: Aligned from the right, the last axes are 3 and 2 — neither is 1, so NumPy raises a ValueError. b[:, None] (shape (2, 1)) would work.

np4.q: A basic slice such as a[1:3] is a copy, so changing it can never change a.
np4.why: Basic slicing returns a view of the same memory. Writing to the slice changes a. Use .copy() for an independent array.

by1.q: If a test is 99% accurate, a positive result means a 99% chance of having the condition.
by1.why: It depends on the base rate. With 0.1% prevalence and 5% false positives, only about 2% of positives are real (lecture 2’s virus example).

by2.q: Naive Bayes assumes the features are conditionally independent given the class.
by2.why: That is the “naive” assumption: P(e₁, …, e_d | B) = ∏ P(eⱼ | B). It is rarely exactly true but often works well.

by3.q: With α-Laplace smoothing (α > 0), a feature value never seen with a class still gets a non-zero likelihood.
by3.why: (0 + α) / (count(B) + mα) is positive, so one unseen combination no longer zeroes the whole product.

by4.q: To classify with naive Bayes you must compute the evidence P(E) in the denominator.
by4.why: P(E) is the same for every class, so it cannot change which class wins. Compare P(B)∏P(eⱼ | B) directly; normalise only if a probability is asked for.

by5.q: A Gaussian likelihood f(x) used in naive Bayes can be greater than 1.
by5.why: It is a density, not a probability. With a small σ the peak 1/(√(2π)σ) exceeds 1 — e.g. σ = 0.1 gives about 3.99.

kn1.q: KNN has no real training phase, but predicting gets slower as the training set grows.
kn1.why: KNN stores the data. Each prediction measures the distance to every stored point, so the cost grows with the data.

kn2.q: Standardizing the features cannot change which points are a test point’s nearest neighbours.
kn2.why: It can. Standardizing rescales each axis, which changes distances — in lecture 3’s T-shirt example the fifth neighbour changes.

kn3.q: With two classes, an odd k avoids ties in the KNN vote.
kn3.why: Two classes and an odd number of votes cannot split evenly.

kn4.q: k = 1 usually gives a smoother decision boundary than k = 15.
kn4.why: The opposite: k = 1 follows every point (jagged, overfitting); a large k averages over many neighbours (smooth, possibly underfitting).

ev1.q: A classifier can have 95% accuracy and 0% recall on the positive class.
ev1.why: With 5 positives in 100, always predicting “negative” is 95% accurate and finds none of the positives.

ev2.q: Precision is the number of true positives divided by everything the model predicted positive.
ev2.why: Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Recall divides by everything that is actually positive: TP / (TP + FN).

ev3.q: D-fold cross-validation on data sorted by class, without shuffling, can give 0% accuracy.
ev3.why: With 4 classes × 20 sorted samples and D = 2, each test fold holds only classes the training fold never saw.

km1.q: K-Means always converges to the clustering with the lowest possible SSE.
km1.why: It always converges, but possibly to a local minimum that depends on the initial centroids.

km2.q: In K-Means, the SSE never increases from one round to the next.
km2.why: Assignment moves points only to closer centroids, and the mean is the best centre for squared distances, so neither step can raise the SSE.

km3.q: A K-Means cluster can end up with no points.
km3.why: A badly placed initial centroid may be nearest to no point at all.

km4.q: The best k for K-Means is the one with the smallest SSE.
km4.why: SSE keeps falling as k grows and reaches 0 at k = n. Use the elbow method instead.

pc1.q: A single perceptron can learn XOR if it is trained for enough epochs.
pc1.why: XOR is not linearly separable, so no line works; the perceptron rule never stops changing the weights.

pc2.q: The perceptron learning rule changes the weights only when the output is wrong.
pc2.why: Δw = η(T − O)x is zero when T = O.

pc3.q: For a sample at x = (0, 0), the perceptron rule can still change the bias θ.
pc3.why: Δw = η(T − O)x is zero, but Δθ = η(T − O) — the bias’s input is always 1.

ml1.q: Stacking several layers with linear activations lets an MLP learn XOR.
ml1.why: A composition of linear maps is linear: W₂(W₁x + c₁) + c₂ is still one line. A non-linear activation is required.

ml2.q: For a two-class problem, the output layer can be one sigmoid unit or two softmax units.
ml2.why: Both give a valid class probability; softmax over two units is equivalent to a sigmoid of the difference.

ml3.q: A dense network 3 → 4 → 2 (with biases) has 26 trainable parameters.

ml4.q: A binary step activation works well with backpropagation.
ml4.why: Its gradient is 0 almost everywhere, so there is nothing to follow. A steep sigmoid σ(cx) approximates it with a usable gradient.

ml5.q: If all weights start at zero, the two hidden neurons of the lecture’s network stay identical during training.
ml5.why: They compute the same value and receive the same δ, so every update is the same — the symmetry is never broken.

im1.q: Flipping an image horizontally changes its grey-level histogram.
im1.why: A flip moves pixels without changing any value, so the histogram is identical.

im2.q: Thresholding and contrast stretching are both point operations.
im2.why: Each output pixel depends only on the same input pixel’s value.

im3.q: Otsu’s method chooses the threshold automatically and gives the same T for the same image every time.
im3.why: That is exactly the advantage the 2024 marking scheme asks for: automatic and reproducible.

im4.q: A suitable 3×3 kernel can flip a 64×64 image horizontally by convolution.
im4.why: A 3×3 kernel only sees a 3×3 neighbourhood, but flipping needs values from up to 63 pixels away.

im5.q: Affine transformations are point-based image operations.
im5.why: The output at (x, y) takes its value from a different position, so it is not a point operation (Final 2022 Q1(f) is false).

im6.q: An affine transformation may preserve distances and angles.
im6.why: Translations, rotations and reflections keep both; scaling and shear do not. “May” makes it true (Final 2024 Q1(f)).

im7.q: Horizontal flipping is a useful augmentation for handwritten digit classification.
im7.why: A mirrored 2 or 7 is not a valid digit. It is useful for cats vs dogs, which is the Final 2022 answer.

im8.q: With M = [[1, 0, 0], [0, −1, rows − 1]], warpAffine turns the image upside down.
im8.why: That is the lecture’s reflection along the x-axis: y′ = −y + (rows − 1), so rows swap and columns stay.

cn1.q: The number of weights in a convolutional layer depends on the input image’s height and width.
cn1.why: It depends on the kernel size, the input depth and the number of filters: (k·k·C_in + 1) × filters.

cn2.q: A 32×32×3 input with ten 5×5 filters, stride 1 and padding 2 gives a 32×32×10 output.
cn2.why: ⌊(32 − 5 + 2·2)/1⌋ + 1 = 32 per side; ten filters give depth 10.

cn3.why: Pooling just takes the maximum (or mean) of each window; there is nothing to learn.

cn4.q: With dilation 2, a 3×3 kernel covers a 5×5 area using 9 weights.
cn4.why: Effective size d(k − 1) + 1 = 5, but there are still 3 × 3 = 9 weights.

cn5.q: Dropout with rate 0.5 also drops units at test time.
cn5.why: Dropout is used only during training; at test time every unit is used.

ab1.q: Alpha-beta pruning can change the move that minimax would choose.
ab1.why: Pruning only skips branches that cannot affect the result; the root value and the chosen move are the same as minimax.

ab2.q: Alpha-beta pruning always prunes at least one branch.
ab2.why: With a bad move order nothing may be pruned — all leaves are examined, still with the same answer.

ab3.q: Examining the best moves first lets alpha-beta prune more of the tree.
ab3.why: Good bounds early make α ≥ β happen sooner, so more branches are cut.

et1.q: Removing the race column from the data guarantees that a model cannot discriminate by race.
et1.why: Proxy features such as postcode can be correlated with race and let the model recover it.

et2.q: Model drift is a reason to keep monitoring a model after it is deployed.
et2.why: As incoming data changes, accuracy can change — monitoring and maintenance is one of the three areas of AI ethics.

formulas.title: Formula sheet
formulas.lead: Every formula the midterms and finals use, in lecture order, with the trap to watch for. Print it, or save it as a PDF.

broadcast.name: Broadcasting rule
broadcast.note: Compare shapes from the right; a length-1 axis stretches. Add axes with None.

pairwise.name: Pairwise distances, expanded
pairwise.note: Lets you build all distances from norms and one matrix product — no (n, m, d) array.

bayes.name: Bayes’ rule
bayes.note: With a rare condition, the posterior is small even for an accurate test.

total.name: Total probability
total.note: The denominator: add every way the evidence can happen.

naive.name: Naive Bayes decision
naive.note: Drop P(E) when you only need the winning class.

laplace.name: α-Laplace smoothing
laplace.note: m is the number of values of this feature, not the number of features.

gauss.name: Gaussian likelihood
gauss.note: Use each class’s own μ and σ. The value can exceed 1.

std.name: Sample standard deviation
std.note: Recent papers print the n − 1 version.

euclid.name: Euclidean distance
euclid.note: Use the distance the question names (some ask for squared or Manhattan).

zscore.name: Standardization
zscore.note: Use the training mean and standard deviation for the test point too.

precision.name: Precision and recall
precision.note: Precision divides by a predicted column, recall by an actual row.

f1.name: F1 score
f1.note: Harmonic mean: small if either P or R is small.

sse.name: K-Means objective (SSE)
sse.note: Never increases between rounds; lowest at k = n, so choose k by the elbow.

centroid.name: Centroid update
centroid.note: An empty cluster keeps its old centroid.

neuron.name: Neuron output
neuron.note: Check whether the step fires at z ≥ 0 or z > 0, and whether outputs are 0/1 or ±1.

perceptron.name: Perceptron learning rule
perceptron.note: Only mistakes change anything; the bias’s input is 1.

sigmoid.name: Sigmoid and its derivative
sigmoid.note: The O(1 − O) factor in every delta.

deltak.name: Output delta
deltak.note: The course writes (O − T) and subtracts in the update.

deltaj.name: Hidden delta
deltaj.note: Use the weights from before this step’s update.

update.name: Weight update
update.note: A zero input means a zero update for that weight.

dense.name: Dense layer parameters
dense.note: +1 for the bias of every output unit.

otsu.name: Otsu’s threshold (lecture 7)
otsu.note: If the paper says one iteration, stop after one.

affine.name: Affine transformation (lecture 7)
affine.note: cv2.warpAffine(img, M, (cols, rows)) — width first in dsize.

reflect.name: Reflections
reflect.note: Reflecting along the x-axis flips the rows (upside down); along the y-axis flips the columns.

rotate.name: Rotation about (x₀, y₀)
rotate.note: The lecture rotates about (cols // 2, rows // 2). Angles go in radians for math.cos, degrees for getRotationMatrix2D.

range.name: Range of a kernel on 8-bit images
range.note: Use it to rescale a filtered image back to 0…255.

outsize.name: Convolution / pooling output size
outsize.note: Floor when it does not divide evenly; “same” padding gives ⌈N/S⌉.

convparams.name: Convolution parameters
convparams.note: Independent of the image size; pooling has none.

dilated.name: Dilated kernel size
dilated.note: Use K_eff in the output-size formula; still K·K weights.

alphabeta.name: Alpha-beta bounds
alphabeta.note: Pruning never changes the root value.
